articles.title: Platform Engineering Maturity Emerges as a Key Differentiator for Enterprise AI Success
articles.text:
Platform engineering maturity is emerging as an important factor in determining whether organizations can turn AI adoption into sustainable operational value, according to Perforce Software's 2026 Platform Engineering Report. The survey of 820 technology professionals found that 73% of organizations it classified as having mature platform engineering practices said platform maturity was a critical or significant factor in their AI success, compared with 44% among less mature organizations. The report also found that 66% of organizations are already using AI in infrastructure workflows, while only 31% report fully autonomous AI, suggesting that most organizations are still navigating the transition from experimentation to governed, production-scale adoption.
The report's broader argument is that AI does not remove the need for strong engineering foundations; it amplifies them. Mature internal developer platforms can provide standardized workflows, automation, governance, policy enforcement, and auditability, giving both developers and AI agents controlled pathways into infrastructure and delivery processes. Perforce reports that organizations with formal governance mechanisms show substantially higher trust in AI than those relying on ad hoc approaches. However, these figures should be interpreted as a correlation from a vendor-sponsored survey rather than proof that platform maturity directly causes higher AI success or trust.
Independent research from Google's DORA program also broadly supports the underlying thesis, although it frames the issue differently. DORA's 2025 research, based on nearly 5,000 technology professionals, describes AI as an "amplifier" that magnifies both organizational strengths and weaknesses. Its findings suggest that high-quality internal platforms help organizations translate individual AI productivity gains into broader delivery improvements, whereas weak platforms can leave those gains trapped behind downstream bottlenecks in testing, security, and deployment. This provides a useful external validation of Perforce's central argument: the value of AI depends heavily on the surrounding engineering system, not simply on the AI tool itself.
Similarly, CNCF and SlashData research points in a similar direction, although it offers a somewhat more nuanced view of platform maturity. Its 2026 Technology Radar found that 35% of organizations use a hybrid platform approach to integrate AI workloads, suggesting that many companies are extending existing developer platforms rather than building entirely separate AI infrastructure. However, only 28% reported having a dedicated platform engineering team, with multi-team collaboration remaining the most common model. This suggests that while platforms are becoming increasingly important to AI adoption, organizations do not necessarily need a highly centralized or fully mature platform engineering function to begin realizing value.
The evidence therefore broadly supports Perforce's conclusion, but it also challenges any overly simple interpretation of the findings. Platform engineering appears to be an important enabler of AI adoption, particularly when it provides reliable automation, clear governance, and fast feedback loops. Still, maturity alone is unlikely to guarantee AI success. The more defensible conclusion is that AI benefits from strong engineering foundations, regardless of exactly how an organization structures its platform function.
The emerging lesson is that AI adoption is increasingly becoming a systems engineering challenge. As AI moves from generating code to operating infrastructure and performing increasingly autonomous tasks, organizations need standardized environments, identity controls, policy enforcement, observability, security, and automated validation to keep that acceleration under control. Perforce's report adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that the organizations most likely to gain durable value from AI will not necessarily be those that deploy the most AI tools or have the highest adoption rates of AI, but those that build the strongest engineering systems around them.

articles.title: NASA puts Crew-13's launch-pad escape in the hands of the 11-times-recalled Cybertruck
articles.text:
Facepalm: If you're an astronaut sitting in a rocket waiting to blast into space, you'd want the reassurance of knowing that a sturdy and reliable vehicle will carry you to safety should the launch encounter problems. This task is usually performed by a heavily armored military personnel carrier, but for the upcoming SpaceX Crew-13 mission, rescue duties will be carried out by the Cybertruck, a vehicle that has been subject to 11 NHTSA recall campaigns.
Making a hasty exit away from the launch pad should something go wrong is important, obviously, but given the potentially destructive power of a rocket, the vehicle coming to astronauts' aid also needs to be sturdy.
NASA uses Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected vehicles (MRAP) in this role. The agency previously said these vehicles' armor is so thick that each door weighs 600 pounds, giving them the sound and feel of a bank vault. This means that even if they aren't moving, they can still act as a bunker.
But for the four astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, their safety will be put in the hands of a Cybertruck. NASA's Richard Jones said that using the EV means NASA doesn't have to organize an MRAP and its crew for the launch. He also noted that this avoids any conflict over resources – SpaceX had been preparing to launch Crew-12 at the same time NASA was preparing a launch attempt for Artemis II.
SpaceX does use Cybertrucks during its own launches. Jones admitted that the vehicles are much quicker than MRAPs for moving astronauts out of danger. They're also easier to drive while wearing gloves.
But Cybertrucks can't exactly compete with MRAPs when it comes to durability. Elon Musk once said that irs Armor Glass could survive baseball-sized hail, but the famous on-stage demo in which a metal ball shattered a window didn't inspire confidence – Musk later claimed hitting the car's body with a sledgehammer in earlier demo weakened the windows. Jones said no modifications had been made to the Cybertruck.
The Cybertruck has been subject to 11 separate US NHTSA safety-recall campaigns for reasons that include an accelerator pedal that could become trapped, wheels that could separate, and drive-inverter failure, none of which you would want to experience while trying to escape an exploding rocket.
The Crew-13's crew is made up of NASA's Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, plus the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. The launch will take place no earlier than 12 September 2026.
The crew will join Expedition 75 aboard the ISS, where it will conduct scientific investigations and technology demonstrations intended to support future missions to the Moon and Mars. Expedition 75's research includes in-space manufacturing, AI- and augmented-reality-assisted health checks, and bioprinting human tissue.

articles.title: Scale Up, Scale Out Challenges Amplified For Clusters
articles.text:
Compute clusters offer more processing capacity but at the cost of higher power. Software is needed to allocate resources effectively and optimize networking and memory.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss changes in AI data center architectures with Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm; Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise; Moshiko Emmer, distinguished engineer at Cadence; Sharad Chole, chief scientist at Expedera; Cameron Brunner, head of HPC development at Siemens EDA; and Sumit Vishwakarma, director of strategic marketing at Synopsys. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is part 2 of a 3-part series. Read part one here.
L-R: Arm’s Bhattacharjee; Axiomise’s Darbari; Cadence’s Emmer; Expedera’s Chole; Siemens EDA’s Brunner; Synopsys’ Vishwakarma.
SE: Compared to the scale up and scale out of racks in a data center, can clusters help reduce power consumption, or do they use more power and are therefore a part of the AI data center’s power problem? Where do clusters sit in the landscape, and what role does software play?
Vishwakarma: You can think of it more like [power consumption] is a growing problem with clusters. That is where it would sit.
Brunner: We’re seeing customers that have racks, and they can’t actually run all their GPUs at full power. They don’t have enough power capacity to run them at full power. A very common thing that we’re working on right now to manage this power usage is identifying power at light [loads], so running GPUs at not max power and looking at the performance you can get out of it. Maybe you can run it at 50%, but it doesn’t double the time it takes, and you get better power per performance. They talk about power per token. Trying to use the software to identify the efficient way to use the hardware can help optimize the output against the power consumption, and that kind of intelligent cluster middleware can drive that type of utilization versus you just throwing all your applications down a machine and saying, ‘Use everything.’
Chole: If I categorize a cluster as a set of nodes that are co-located or connected in some special way, rather than just connected to the typical data center networking, then this problem becomes about whether there is a benefit to using a cluster topology rather than using a general cloud topology. The applications that can benefit from either scale-up or scale-out applications that are getting bottlenecked by just staying under a single server are the ones that get the benefit of going and using clusters as a whole. HPC AI is a typical use case. You can even have database systems that are close to the storage systems, and they are serving them through some sort of APIs. Another example is financial systems that have to do very low-latency prediction, so they are much more amenable to having a very dedicated connectivity, and uptime also needs to be very high. This gives some reason to actually build the clusters. I also want to separate the software clustering effort from the hardware clustering effort, because what we are doing on hardware clusters is basically connecting nodes in a way where there is a predefined topology. You have to reconfigure or rewire the data center again to be able to change that. But the software allocation and utilization of those pieces, or the slicing of that hardware cluster into software or virtual groups, is a different problem.
SE: With power trade-offs, where operators might say, ‘We’re not going to run the GPU at max,’ how do they calculate how much to push the GPU?
Brunner: In terms of the application, how you partition and monitor the hardware, and how you’re running your applications, provides a lot of additional value. To solve the [power] problem we just discussed, you need to know and see the history of previous workloads at run time. You need to monitor how work has been going through the system, and you’ll see through your results — you can do experiments on your cluster with your workloads — what the best outcomes would be. This is also a place where artificial intelligence, plugged into the metrics and the control of the HPC system, can really start automating a lot of this process, and it’s something Nvidia is really big on: power control. You can even identify different power performance profiles that you see per individual GPUs in a given cluster, so being able to steer workloads to specific machines that have different performance profiles is a feasible thing. I think AI will help really enable some of that automation. Right now, a human can do it with the tools that we have. It’s a little more work with more manual experimentation.
Bhattacharjee: Power is becoming the bottleneck now. Initially, it was the GPU availability and the like, but now it is coming down to power. There are a lot of interesting innovations going on to make sure that the power consumed is at a reasonable limit, by which you can scale. What we are seeing is that instead of having just GPUs do all the work, there is now a close orchestration between the CPU and the GPU in the system, and people are realizing that as you move from training to inference, the workload pattern is completely different. Training is all about crunching numbers — matrix multiplications across those several cores that are running on the GPU, and they are running at the highest frequency to get the best training outcome. However, if you go to inference, especially now with the agents coming in, agents are supposed to do people’s work at a much faster cadence. They are booking Uber rides for you, or booking flights for you, or doing some research. Those are not matrix multiplication and crunching number tasks. Those run very well on CPUs. What we are seeing is that there are a lot of workloads that are now running on CPUs, and when they’re running on CPUs, the GPUs can be at a lower power, and the CPUs are basically taking the workload hit, and they’re running it at a much lower power compared to the GPUs. Once they’re done, they hand it over to the accelerators for a certain portion where there is some reasoning work required, which does need an accelerator, so the GPU or a custom accelerator does the work at that time.
The GPU is the one that is taking the power, so there’s close power coordination as the workload shifts from the CPU to the GPU. A good example is what Nvidia has done with Grace Hopper or Vera Rubin. There are a lot of innovations happening to create an equivalent system to scale this across, because you can’t rely on one company to do everything. It’s going to go along a similar paradigm to where the CPU and GPUs work together, and now you can think about scaling it up across the rack and scaling out across multiple of those. The CPU has started taking a very central role in terms of how these workloads are being served, especially as the shift is happening from training to inference. Inference, as far as our understanding goes, is going to be +80% of the AI workloads going forward, as the models are getting more measured, so the training is at a stage where people are saying, ‘These are great for deployment,’ and as soon as you deploy, it’s all inference.
Brunner: It’s really important to talk about that transition from training to inference, and also the types of use cases that we’re asking the cluster to do. An inference workload is likely real-time, where somebody is waiting for that response. The training workload is more like a batch workload. Let’s say you’ve got eight hours. You submit it at night because it needs to be done when you get into work the next day. We can run at lower power over the evening, whereas we’re maybe always running inference at higher power. It’s another way of looking at using categories of the types of workloads that you’re running and the time you expect to get out of them, in terms of how you might want to steer power consumption.
Emmer: Clusters don’t solve the power problem by themselves. They can actually magnify it if the architecture causes too much data movement. The win comes when we use architectural specialization intelligently — CPU for control and orchestration, accelerators for dense math, local memory for hot data, and the interconnect only for traffic that truly needs to escape the node. So the metric I’d focus on is not raw power, but useful work per joule across the full hierarchy, or performance-per-watt.
SE: When it comes to interconnects, I/Os, and data flow, are there different challenges between rack scale up, scale out, and compute clusters, or are they similar?
Darbari: A cluster changes the design problem from building a powerful machine to engineering a coordinated distributed system. In a single server, the main concerns are typically local compute, memory, and I/O balance. In a cluster, performance depends heavily on workload partitioning, communication patterns, and whether the interconnect can carry synchronization and data movement efficiently.
Vishwakarma: The architect needs to think about the cluster as one unit and not just design the silicon for that specific package, so networking is the biggest bottleneck. You are as fast as your slowest network switch. Think about how fast the workloads are changing. As we’re doing more inferencing, it is not like training where I’m looking for one big compute, and nobody is interrupting me. Inferencing is when somebody is waiting for the response. You give a query to your GPT or any other model, and you’re expecting it to come back, and then you query another. There’s so much traffic going in, so the network problem and latency specifically have ballooned with the new workloads. What needs to be addressed is that you want the lowest latency for the traffic, not only within the chip. And the chip itself is evolving. Now the chip is not just a single die. It is a multi-die chip with two dies that talk to each other. There are 3D-ICs. So the signals are traveling from between the dies, all the way to the signals traversing between two nodes. Everything adds to the latency. We are looking at this problem of die-to-die communication, where we have the UCIe kind of IPs for the fast data communication, all the way to Ethernet and UALink for cross communication between the nodes.
SE: How does the memory usage change for clusters compared to racks?
Bhattacharjee: The problem that we are trying to solve is how to execute the workload at the lowest latency possible. If you look at the CPUs and the GPUs, they are usually inside the server. Today, the typical form factor is two CPUs connected to eight GPUs — that’s a sweet form factor. This might change in the future, to have different ratios, but if you look at the CPUs and break them down, the CPU has the fastest memory, which is L2 cache. Nowadays, you have CPUs with hundreds of cores, and each core has a dedicated L2 cache attached to it, which is the fastest cache that it can access. These are in nanoseconds. Whatever job it can do by holding things in this L2 cache, that’s what it’ll do, but it’s usually small in size, because it’s per core, typically in the one to two megabyte range. Then you have shared L3 cache, which is shared across all the cores. Let’s say a CPU has 128 cores, then all the 128 cores can now access the shared cache, and that shared cache is also typically one to two megabytes per core. If there are 128 cores, you have 128 megabytes of cache. It’s still small. We’re still talking about megabytes, but it’s some of the fastest access that the cores have now.
If you go out, and you have the DDR or the main memory attached, that’s much bigger. The DDRs are typically in the gigabyte range, so, depending on what the CPU supports, if it’s 12 DDR, you are now talking about tons of gigabytes of memory that is attached. That’s going to be slower compared to the caches, but much faster. Now we are talking about the millisecond range. Then there’s a link between the CPU and the GPU, and you want to make sure that the CPU can push the traffic as fast as possible to the accelerator for processing, and that’s where the link comes in.
Nvidia has done a good job in coming up with NVLink, which allows it to push traffic at a much faster cadence over the physical link. There’s a physical limit, of course. It’s done with the PCIe connection, and that has some limits, but they are doing interesting stuff using AMBA CHI, which is an open standard to move the traffic. As Sumit mentioned, there’s an industry-wide initiative to make that a standard, so that all the different CPUs and all the different accelerators can take a similar kind of speed-up approach. Then, if you go to the accelerator part, HBM (high bandwidth memory) is super fast, and that’s what the GPUs and accelerators normally use to process the traffic. But, again, it’s smaller in size, and it’s very expensive, so interesting innovations are going on, especially for a swarm of agents with multiple models in a mixture of experts (MoE), where you have multiple models doing different work, and one is handing over tasks to another. Can you now keep some of these contexts, which are called KV cache, in the larger memory when the agent is not active, and then push them back to the accelerator memory when it’s active? There’s a lot of innovation going on the software side to ensure that the system-level efficiency comes in. This is a huge topic. When you’re talking about efficiency at a cluster level, it’s a combination of software, hardware, interconnects, cache, and memory; all of that comes together, and then there is the networking aspect as well.
Brunner: That’s the big challenge when you go from one machine. It’s such a great breakdown of all of the challenges in a single machine, so it becomes another whole set of challenges, and another whole set of technology to start linking the machines together. There have been a lot of strategies with that over time. We have our low-latency networks — the big, common ones are (HPE) Slingshot and InfiniBand (from Mellanox, acquired by Nvidia). Then it’s a case of, how do you hook up a large number of machines? It’s kind of a simple problem. Get an InfiniBand switch and put it on a rack, plug in all the machines, and then all those machines are pretty quickly connected via their interconnect. Well, let’s say you have 500 racks. There isn’t a 500-port switch. How do you put all the racks together so you don’t incorporate bottlenecks? HPE has a strategy called Dragonfly Network Topology, which kind of tries to maximize utilization of the interconnect, so you don’t put bottlenecks in when you have a large collaborative job over a lot of machines in the environment. Because what they found was that the original type of strategies is hierarchical, where you would have a rack with all of its nodes, another rack with all of its nodes, and then let’s trunk those racks together. But now if you have a job that’s split between two racks, it saturates that connection and everything goes away, so this is a big, a big challenge.
Emmer: The biggest mistake is to think that scale-up and scale-out are just the same problem at different sizes. They’re different latency and bandwidth regimes. Scale-up is about preserving locality and reducing serialization/deserialization overhead. Scale-out is about minimizing synchronization penalties and containing traffic amplification. Inside the package, I can design for extremely high bandwidth and fine-grain communication. Across a node, I’m already paying a different cost. Across racks, the system must become much more selective about what traffic is truly latency critical. So architectural efficiency comes from keeping the right data local: weights, activations, KV cache, metadata, and control traffic. And only exporting what must move. At the cluster scale, performance is often determined less by peak compute and more by where the data is forced to travel.
Darbari: For a chip architect, the lower‑layer links matter because their bandwidth, latency, ordering guarantees, and failure behavior shape what the higher layers can realistically deliver. Above that come node-level fabrics and then inter-node networking across the wider cluster. Correctness becomes harder as well. A server is one tightly coupled failure domain, while a cluster consists of many independent components that can fail, restart, or become unreachable while the overall service continues running. That means architects must think in terms of protocols, distributed state, and recovery semantics rather than only local functional behavior.

articles.title: Rubrik unveils Agent Identity to govern AI agents one tool call at a time - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Rubrik unveils Agent Identity to govern AI agents one tool call at a time
Rubrik Inc. today unveiled Rubrik Agent Identity, a service that governs what artificial intelligence agents are allowed to do by granting access one tool call at a time. The company announced the service at the Black Hat conference in Las Vegas.
The service is an expansion of Rubrik Agent Cloud, the agent governance platform the company launched in October and made generally available for Anthropic PBC’s Claude in June. Agent Identity targets the credential layer beneath those deployments. Agents typically inherit the broad, standing permissions built for human employees, which means a single compromised or misbehaving agent can act destructively across software-as-a-service applications, databases and application programming interfaces before anyone notices.
“Agents are no longer just synthesizing information, they are acting on the enterprise on behalf of employees, and the access models we built for humans and static credentials were never designed for autonomous actors,” said Dev Rishi, general manager of AI at Rubrik. “Agent Identity lets enterprises decide who can do what with agents and enforces it per tool call, at the moment of action, with scoped, short-lived access and no standing permissions.”
Rubrik is pitching the problem as a “shadow workforce” of unmonitored machine identities. According to research from Rubrik Zero Labs, 86% of global information technology and security leaders expect AI agents to outpace their organization’s security guardrails within the next year, while only 23% say they have full visibility into the agents already running in their environments.
Agent Identity works across three functions: monitoring every agent and Model Context Protocol server at runtime, controlling access per tool call using fine-tuned models and remediating risky actions through identity, audit logs and Rubrik’s Agent Rewind feature. Customers start by building an inventory of active agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins, then scope access to specific servers and tools by user and group using On-Behalf-Of federation, which extends existing identity structures rather than replacing them. Standing permissions are eliminated by minting scoped, short-lived tokens for each individual tool call.
Enforcement happens at an MCP gateway. Every tool call clears three checkpoints before it executes: a behavioral analysis step in which Rubrik’s SAGE governance engine evaluates the intent, input parameters and likely operational impact of the request, a policy check at the infrastructure layer and an identity verification step that authenticates the agent session and issues the token scoped to that call. An unauthorized action, such as a write or modification outside an explicit policy scope, is blocked before execution.
For actions that clear the gateway and still go wrong, Agent Rewind reverses them. Rubrik has described the feature as the only one of its kind on the market. The company’s own survey work found 88% of leaders are worried about meeting recovery time objectives as agentic threats scale.
Agent Identity integrates with Okta Inc. and Microsoft Corp.’s Entra ID, extending enterprise identities to machine actors without standing up a separate directory. Rubrik did not disclose pricing or a general availability date.
Rubrik, which now describes itself as “the Security and AI Operations Company,” moved into agent tooling in earnest with its acquisition of Predibase Inc. in a deal worth between $100 million and $500 million in June 2025. Rishi co-founded Predibase and served as its chief executive.

articles.title: What killed your startup? (Live from Startupfest)
articles.text:
It is an immutable law of entrepreneurship that more startups fail than succeed. That’s both a warning and the price of admission for any founder.
But it’s not fate, either. And knowing why most startups fail can be helpful in ensuring your startup succeeds.
“There has never been a more exciting time to found and build a company in Canada.”
Melissa Nightingale
Success, failure, and the lessons learned from both were hot topics at our live edition of The BetaKit Podcast, recorded at the Startupfest village in Montréal’s Grand Quay in July. Featuring a killer lineup of Startupfest speakers (see list below), we discussed the leading causes of startup demise, playbooks for company scaling, and the potential of AI to be a catalyst for both.
The omnipresence of AI throughout the conversation (recorded in a very fun rapid-fire talk show format) wasn’t just because we had a director from the Canadian research hub, Vector Institute, on the panel. AI has saturated companies across verticals and business units, but like any tool, it can be used in beneficial or harmful ways. The conversational contrast between AI being used as an excuse to treat employees as less than people in one example, and a superpower helping small teams scale beyond their means in the next, was not lost on this humble live podcast moderator.
Subscribe: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Overcast, Pocket Casts, RSS
So, how can founders best use the means at their disposal to keep their companies alive and thriving? Let’s dig in!

articles.title: Catching rogue AI behavior with identity-aware analytics
articles.text:
Catching rogue AI behavior with identity-aware analytics
Ming Lu, Kenny Johnson, and Ayush Kumar
When you look at your AI bill, it can be hard to tell if anything is amiss. You first need a baseline so you can see what has changed, whether it’s an agent that’s gone wild or an employee whose usage has spiked 10x. Being able to spot those shifts lets you start investigating, and so far, it’s been hard to see them.
Knowing who is doing what with AI is one of the key challenges organizations are confronting right now. One report from Stanford University found that 59% of organizations said knowledge gaps were their biggest obstacle to responsible AI governance.
This is a security problem as much as a financial one. Solving these issues takes two things: a verified identity on every request (so a spike has a name behind it), and a picture of what normal looks like for that identity. Today we're announcing both.
Identity-aware AI Gateway with Cloudflare Access is now in open beta, and User Insights is generally available to every AI Gateway customer at no additional cost. Together they turn the traffic already flowing through AI Gateway into a behavioral baseline for every person and agent using it, and identify the ones that break from it.
What is AI Gateway?
AI Gateway is the central control plane for all of your AI usage. Instead of every app and team calling models on OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or Workers AI directly, requests route through AI Gateway first, giving you one place to observe, secure, and govern all your AI usage.
It works with the applications you build, and with the coding tools your developers already live in. Route agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot through AI Gateway, and they fall under the same visibility and controls as everything else.
Identity-aware AI Gateway
With the AI Gateway and Cloudflare Access integration, you can put a custom domain in front of your gateway and protect it with Access, just like any other application. That means you can:
- Authenticate with any SAML-supported identity provider, like Okta or Entra, removing the need to generate and pass around Cloudflare API keys.
- Set policies on exactly who can access your gateway.
- Send requests to a clean hostname like ai.example.com , with no account ID or gateway ID in the URL.
Every authenticated request now carries the user's identity from Access. AI Gateway adds the verified Access user ID to request metadata as cf.user_id, so you can filter logs, analytics, and spend by the person who actually made the request.
Coupled with spend limits, that identity becomes a budgeting tool. Because each request now carries a real user, you can set per-user spend limits: give every user their own budget bucket, then block further requests or fall back to a cheaper model when they hit it. No more surprise invoices, and no shared API key hiding who spent what.
One of our early adopters, Flexport, ran into exactly this problem.
"Shared API keys make it almost impossible to tell who is using an AI service or apply the access rules we already have for employees,” says Max Baumgarten, Staff Security Engineer at Flexport. “Putting Cloudflare Access in front of AI Gateway gives each request an authenticated identity and lets us use our existing identity policies at the gateway. Our teams can adopt AI tools without creating a separate authentication system for every client."
In the near future, you'll be able to use your users' identity provider groups to set spend limits or control which models a group can access. For example, give your machine learning team access to frontier models, cap the spend of your support team, or scope a budget to everyone working on a specific project, all mapped to the groups you already manage in your identity provider.
The new User Insights tab
Within AI Gateway, you will now see a tab called User Insights. User Insights reads the traffic passing through your gateway and turns it into a behavioral picture of every account. It learns how each account normally acts, identifies the ones that break from that pattern, and gives you the context to tell a rogue agent from a busy engineer. It works on the traffic already going through your gateway, so there's nothing to set up.
User Insights tracks cost, including where it's being wasted, such as low cache-hit rates and oversized context windows. Plenty of tools already do that. What they don't do is tell you whether an account is behaving normally. That's what we chose to focus on, alongside cost controls.
Baselining every account: people and agents
Every account leaves a behavioral fingerprint over time, whether it's a person or agent. An agent summarizing tickets every three hours is tight and consistent. A person is messier, with varied prompts, irregular timing, and long sessions on hard problems. Both are legitimate, so the same deviation can be noise for one and a real signal for the other.
In User Insights, we start by scoring sessions, not single requests. Absolute thresholds fail here: a $500 jump from a heavy user might be normal, while a $50 session from an agent that always spends $5 is a 10x change that could otherwise slip by. So we compare each session against the account's own history, using its 95th percentile (p95) session cost over the last 30 days. That gives us a read on how the account normally operates, and anything above 2x of its p95 is a strong candidate for anomalous behavior.
The following analysis outlines how we arrived at these numbers.
Figure 1: Session Cost Anomaly Detection
How to read the chart above
The chart plots real sessions from our own internal traffic. Each point represents an individual session (plotted on log scales):
- X-axis (Session Cost): Total cost in dollars.
- Y-axis (x User p95): How many times the session exceeded the user's personal baseline.
The two dashed threshold lines divide the sessions into four categories:
- Top-Right (★ Stars): Exceeds both the 2x user p95 baseline and the account-level p99 ceiling. These are high relative spikes that represent meaningful abnormal spend and will trigger an alert.
- Top-Left: High relative spike (2x user p95), but below the account p99 floor. We ignore this to avoid alerting on small-dollar shifts.
- Bottom-Right: High absolute spend, but consistent with this user's typical high usage. This is also ignored as routine behavior.
- Bottom-Left: Normal activity well within both baselines.
Figure 2: Account-level Session Cost Distribution
This histogram (Figure 2) maps every session cost across the organization to establish an account-wide ceiling:
- Typical Usage: The vast majority of sessions cost well under $10, with the 95th percentile sitting at $20.
- Account p99 ($200): Only 1% of all sessions across the entire company reach or exceed $200.
So why did we pick p99? Setting our absolute dollar ceiling at the account p99 creates a meaningful bar. It guarantees that an anomaly isn't just a sudden shift for one specific user, but also ranks among the most expensive 1% of sessions across the entire organization.
Figure 3: Single User Session History
Baselines aren't static. As an account's habits change, its rolling p95 (green line) and 2x threshold (orange line) move with it, so an alert always reflects recent behavior rather than a number set once. We also apply a dollar floor so that a spike has to be both statistically unusual and worth an admin’s time to investigate. That dollar floor is what keeps a micro-user's 500x blip over a few cents from ever firing an alert.
The right lens for detecting rogue behavior
After all the analysis above, what admins see is a view of the accounts that broke their own pattern with everything normal filtered out. That filtered view is a rogue behavior feed.
This behavior is hard to catch because the signal is never a new tool or a blocked action. It's a trusted account doing more of what it's already allowed to do. It might be a service account that suddenly starts running more expensive sessions, or a person whose usage jumps well past their own norm and stays there for days.
None of these trip a policy, but all of them break a behavioral baseline. A sudden departure from an account's own usage is often the first observable sign of a compromised credential or an agent going off the rails.
User Insights does not decide intent, and it does not block anyone; instead, it puts the handful of accounts that started behaving strangely in front of an admin so someone can ask the next question. Sometimes that leads to a real investigation. Sometimes it just means that someone needs coaching (like the developer who dumps a whole codebase into every prompt when a snippet would do).
What's next
We’ll help you move from cost control to cost optimization
Once you’ve set a budget, the natural next question is: how can you get the equivalent output quality at lower cost? Not every request needs a frontier model. A summarization task or a simple code completion can run on a cheaper model without meaningful quality loss.
We're building task-based smart routing, where AI Gateway analyzes the incoming request and routes it to the model that gives you the best result at the lowest cost. At the organizational level, you’ll be able to see where you can capture the most savings by routing to more efficient models.Task-based smart routing is in active development. We'll share more as it matures.
We’ll help you understand how AI is being used
Anomaly detection tells you an account broke its pattern, but not why. An admin still has to dig into the logs and piece together what happened. Closing that gap is what we're focused on next, and it starts with classifying what the traffic actually is.
We're building prompt classification that sorts requests into categories like coding, writing, and others. These categories are the context missing from almost every other signal. A spend spike in “coding” from an engineer might be acceptable, but the same spike in a category that account has never touched is not. Classification can show an organization not just how much AI it uses, but what it uses AI for.
It also answers the question underneath most of these conversations: is AI being used for the work it was intended? Once business traffic is separated from everything else, personal use becomes visible. From the outside, someone running a side hustle on company time and someone quietly moving data out through a model look the same. Telling them apart is central to catching insider risk.
Once your AI traffic is running through AI Gateway, each new category of risk or efficiency signal is one more thing an admin gets with no extra setup.
Get started
User Insights is generally available today to every AI Gateway customer at no additional cost. It's already in the dashboard for anyone sending traffic through the gateway, so if you're already routing through AI Gateway, this view is available to you.
If you haven't already, create a gateway and start making requests to any model in our catalog.
We recommend that you put AI Gateway behind Cloudflare Access which is now in open beta. The spend and anomaly views work without it, but attaching an identity is what turns an anonymous account ID into a name you can actually act on. Start in monitoring mode to learn your baselines before you enforce anything.
We want to hear how you're managing AI today. Join the conversation on Discord or reach out to your account team.

articles.title: I test smart glasses for a living and even ignoring privacy problems there’s too many reasons you shouldn’t buy cheap Meta Ray-Ban alternatives
articles.text:
Budget Meta Ray-Ban alternatives are selling out in stores — but please don’t buy them
Not so smart
- Cheap smart glasses are selling out as people look for Meta Ray-Ban alternatives
- More camera glasses are leading to more privacy concerns for many
- I wouldn't buy them for plenty of other reasons
If you want a pair of smart glasses, you’re spoiled for choice in terms of what they can do technologically, and over time we’ve seen more and more budget options appear. These cheaper models are the first step in making emerging gadgets more accessible, but for smart specs there’s a fear they might simply exacerbate the growing concerns over the tech.
Australian discount store Kmart recently went viral after the AU$89 Anko glasses it was selling sold out entirely (via The Guardian). In the US and UK, you don’t have to look far to find equally affordable camera glasses available through reputable digital marketplaces such as Amazon.
Given the proven popularity of Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley specs, it’s no surprise the market would see an influx of smart glasses, especially cheap pairs that aim to mimic much more expensive rivals while keeping costs low — typically by downgrading their technological capabilities and not partnering with premium design brands.
However, cheap smart glasses aren’t as universally celebrated as cheap TVs or affordable smartphones — scrolling through online forums discussing this news, the replies aren’t kind about smart glasses, discussing the pitfalls of smart glasses in general and more affordable options specifically.
The most prominent concern is that cheap camera glasses expand the range of people with the technology. More people with these glasses means more people possibly recording people in public without their knowledge.
There are also fears that cheap camera glasses might not come with the same sophisticated tamper protection glasses from more recognizable brands boast. Either through tape coverings or minor electrical modifications, folks could disable the camera light and use the specs even more covertly than they otherwise would — they’ve tried the same with Meta specs, but Meta has patched out these workarounds so far.
Privacy and other problems
Beyond the impact on the general public, cheap smart glasses users might want to consider the privacy implications of wearing cameras from unknown brands.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
We’ve seen that even super well-known brands like Meta aren’t perfect — for example, there are reports that contractors could see videos (including intimate or otherwise private content) taken using the glasses if it involved the AI in some way — so why should we expect completely unknown brands with nothing to lose to be any better with privacy?
In fact, considering their lack of notoriety makes them less likely to get investigated in the way Meta was by journalists who uncovered the sharing of videos with contractors. The ease with which tiny brands can dissolve and pop back up under different names, I for one would be a lot less trusting of what they do with my data and of their phone apps.
Of course, many lesser-known brands behave responsibly, but when there’s so much room for things to go wrong, for private information or video to get leaked, I just have this extra layer of paranoia I can’t shake.
Even ignoring my personal privacy concerns, as someone who has tested countless smart glasses at this point, I’ve found that better-known brands are simply better at making hardware and software.
I’ve worn so many uncomfortable specs with tinny audio, awful camera quality, terrible AI, and apps that are worse than useless. They’re sluggish. They’re ugly. They’re not worth even a budget price.
Just don’t buy them.
If you do want smart specs, save up for something proper — it doesn’t have to be from Meta, but I’d recommend choosing a brand with plenty of solid independent reviews. While I’m using them less for reasons better explained by other writing, I have gone weeks on end wearing a good pair of smart glasses thanks to comfy yet fashionable design and solid tech. Whereas the cheap (and terrible) glasses I’ve tried I’ve wanted to rip off my face within hours.
You get what you pay for.

Hamish is a Senior Staff Writer for TechRadar and you’ll see his name appearing on articles across nearly every topic on the site from smart home deals to speaker reviews to graphics card news and everything in between. He uses his broad range of knowledge to help explain the latest gadgets and if they’re a must-buy or a fad fueled by hype. Though his specialty is writing about everything going on in the world of virtual reality and augmented reality.

articles.title: Las mejores series turcas en Netflix (en 2026), del amor al thriller
articles.text:
El catálogo turco de la plataforma ha dejado de ser un apéndice de las telenovelas que llegaron a la televisión española hace una década. Lo que reúne esta selección de las mejores series turcas en Netflix son producciones pensadas para temporadas cortas, con episodios de menos de una hora y arcos que se cierran, bastante lejos de las tramas interminables que popularizaron el género.
Hay patrones que ayudan a orientarse. Estambul aparece como escenario en casi todas, aunque unas la usen como decorado de época y otras como ciudad contemporánea. Y hay nombres que vuelven, desde Berkun Oya hasta Umur Turagay, responsables de varias de las piezas más personales del listado. La mayoría son miniseries o series de dos y tres temporadas, así que el conjunto funciona igual para una tarde suelta que para un plan más largo.
El sastre (2023)
Género Drama, thriller psicológico. Nota FilmAffinity 4,8. Temporadas 3. Episodios 23.
Peyami dirige una sastrería de prestigio en Estambul y arrastra un legado familiar que preferiría no haber heredado. El encargo que lo desestabiliza llega de su mejor amigo, que le pide coser el vestido de novia de su prometida, y a partir de ahí El sastre se convierte en un juego de secretos compartidos entre los tres. La serie adapta una novela de la psiquiatra Gülseren Budayıcıoğlu construida sobre casos reales de consulta, y ese origen se nota en el interés por la culpa y el silencio familiar más que por el enredo. El acabado visual sostiene buena parte del atractivo, con un vestuario y una dirección artística cuidados al detalle. Concluyó en su tercera temporada.
Creada por Onur Güvenatam. Con Çağatay Ulusoy, Şifanur Gül, Salih Bademci, Olgun Şimşek y Berrak Tüzünataç.
Mi otra yo (2022-2026)
Género Drama, romance. Nota FilmAffinity 6,3. Temporadas 3. Episodios 24.
Ayvalık, en la costa turca, es el destino al que viajan tres amigas cuando a una de ellas le diagnostican una enfermedad grave y decide probar un tratamiento alternativo. Ada es cirujana, Sevgi abogada y Leyla ha dedicado su vida entera a la familia, y Mi otra yo aprovecha esa estancia para que las tres revisen los traumas heredados de sus linajes. Nuran Evren Şit ha escrito la serie completa desde el primer episodio, lo que explica su tono sostenido y un ritmo pausado más cercano al drama de sanación que al melodrama. La luz mediterránea y los olivos funcionan como parte del relato. Cerró su historia en una tercera temporada de ocho episodios.
Creada por Nuran Evren Şit. Con Tuba Büyüküstün, Seda Bakan, Boncuk Yılmaz, Rıza Kocaoğlu y Murat Boz.
Las alas de la ambición (2022-2024)
Género Drama, thriller laboral. Nota FilmAffinity 5,4. Temporadas 3. Episodios 24.
Meriç Acemi construye aquí un duelo entre dos mujeres que se necesitan y se detestan a partes iguales. Lale Kıran es la presentadora más respetada del informativo de máxima audiencia y Aslı Tuna, la becaria que entra en su equipo con una ambición que va bastante más allá de aprender el oficio. Las alas de la ambición convierte una redacción de televisión en un campo de batalla donde cada favor tiene precio y cada titular es un movimiento calculado. Funciona porque no reparte razones ni condena a ninguna de las dos, y porque el guion entiende cómo se ejerce el poder dentro de un medio audiovisual. Concluyó en su tercera temporada.
Creada por Meriç Acemi y dirigida por Deniz Yorulmazer. Con Birce Akalay, Miray Daner, İbrahim Çelikkol, İrem Sak y Burak Yamantürk.
Medianoche en el Pera Palace (2022-2024)
Género Fantástico, misterio, drama. Nota FilmAffinity 5,8. Temporadas 2. Episodios 16.
El Pera Palace de Estambul es un hotel real y ese edificio sostiene una de las propuestas más atípicas entre las mejores series turcas en Netflix. Una periodista que investiga su historia acaba desplazada al pasado, donde descubre una trama capaz de alterar el rumbo del país. Medianoche en el Pera Palace parte de un libro de no ficción de Charles King sobre el establecimiento y aprovecha ese material para moverse entre el relato de espionaje y la fantasía de viajes en el tiempo. Hazal Kaya sostiene los dos registros temporales sin que el conjunto pierda credibilidad, y la ambientación de ambas épocas está trabajada con detalle. Se despidió en su segunda temporada.
Creada por Emre Şahin, Kelly McPherson y Sam Anzel. Con Hazal Kaya, Selahattin Paşalı, Tansu Biçer y James Chalmers.
Cruce (2016)
Género Drama, romance. Nota FilmAffinity 5,6. Temporadas 3. Episodios 31.
Un empresario del automóvil, una doctora de gran talento y un joven que busca su lugar en el mundo comparten un suceso que reordena las tres biografías. Cruce arranca desde ese punto de encuentro para desplegar un melodrama de clases sociales, matrimonios infelices y decisiones antiguas que vuelven, con Estambul y sus contrastes como telón de fondo. Es la producción más antigua de esta selección y también la más extensa, con una estructura heredada de la televisión generalista turca antes de que las plataformas impusieran temporadas cortas. İbrahim Çelikkol y Belçim Bilgin sostienen el eje sentimental. Quien llegue desde dramas breves notará el cambio de ritmo en el primer episodio.
Dirigida por Ömer Faruk Sorak, Gökçen Usta Çaylar y Deniz Yorulmazer. Con İbrahim Çelikkol, Belçim Bilgin, Alican Yücesoy, Rojda Demirer y Ayda Aksel.
Gracias, ¿el siguiente? (2024)
Género Comedia romántica, drama. Nota FilmAffinity 4,9. Temporadas 3. Episodios 24.
Leyla Taylan es una abogada de éxito que encaja una ruptura dolorosa y decide asomarse al mundo de las citas contemporáneas con sus amigas como red de seguridad. Gracias, ¿el siguiente? se mueve en la comedia romántica urbana y sabe que su terreno es el de las aplicaciones, los desencuentros y las conversaciones de grupo, no el del gran amor contrariado. Ece Yörenç firma la creación y le imprime un tono ligero que no renuncia a los momentos incómodos. Serenay Sarıkaya carga con la mayor parte del carisma de la serie y encuentra un registro cómico que su trayectoria dramática no dejaba prever. Suma tres temporadas de ocho episodios cada una.
Creada por Ece Yörenç y dirigida por Bertan Başaran. Con Serenay Sarıkaya, Fatih Artman, Hakan Kurtaş, Boran Kuzum y Ahmet Rıfat Şungar.
Amor 101 (2020-2021)
Género Comedia, romance, adolescente. Nota FilmAffinity 6,3. Temporadas 2. Episodios 16.
Estambul, finales de los años ochenta. Cuatro estudiantes marginados de un instituto ven cómo la única profesora que los defiende empieza a recibir presiones para marcharse, y deciden que la forma de retenerla es encontrarle un amor. Amor 101 sale de esa premisa disparatada con bastante más sensibilidad de la esperada, porque el objetivo real de la operación es que ellos aprendan algo sobre sí mismos. Meriç Acemi escribe una nostalgia de instituto que funciona sin subrayados, apoyada en un reparto joven bien dirigido y en una banda sonora de época. Cerró su historia en una segunda temporada y es una de las entradas más ligeras del conjunto.
Creada por Meriç Acemi. Con Mert Yazıcıoğlu, Kubilay Aka, Alina Boz, Pınar Deniz y Selahattin Paşalı.
The Gift (2019-2021)
Género Drama, misterio, fantástico. Nota FilmAffinity 5,6. Temporadas 3. Episodios 24.
Atiye es pintora, tiene la vida encauzada y está a punto de casarse cuando un arqueólogo le habla de un símbolo aparecido en la excavación de un templo antiguo, el mismo motivo que ella dibuja sin saber por qué. The Gift convierte ese hallazgo en un viaje hacia el origen de su propia familia, con un componente místico que sostiene la intriga sin devorar el drama. Ozan Açıktan dirige con una paleta fría que contrasta con la luz de los exteriores. Fue una de las primeras producciones originales del catálogo turco y sigue funcionando como puerta de entrada cómoda a las mejores series turcas en Netflix. Concluyó en su tercera temporada.
Dirigida por Ozan Açıktan. Con Beren Saat, Mehmet Günsür, Metin Akdülger y Melisa Şenolsun.
Hakan, el protector (2018-2020)
Género Fantástico, acción. Nota FilmAffinity 4,9. Temporadas 4. Episodios 32.
Antes de que el catálogo turco se llenara de dramas de autor, la plataforma probó con una fantasía urbana de superhéroes. Hakan trabaja en una tienda de Estambul hasta que descubre su vínculo con una orden secreta encargada de proteger la ciudad frente a los Inmortales, un enemigo que lleva siglos operando en la sombra. Hakan, el protector combina acción, mitología local y una lectura muy física del escenario, con persecuciones por cubiertas, cisternas y callejones del casco antiguo. Binnur Karaevli creó la serie y la sostuvo durante cuatro temporadas, las suficientes para cerrar el arco completo del personaje sin dejar cabos pendientes.
Creada por Binnur Karaevli. Con Çağatay Ulusoy, Ayça Ayşin Turan, Hazar Ergüçlü, Mehmet Kurtuluş y Okan Yalabık.
Şahmaran (2023-2024)
Género Fantástico, drama, romance. Nota FilmAffinity 5,2. Temporadas 2. Episodios 14.
La leyenda de Şahmaran, la reina de las serpientes, circula por Anatolia desde hace siglos y aquí se convierte en el motor de un relato contemporáneo. Şahsu viaja a Adana para dar unas clases y, sobre todo, para encarar al abuelo que abandonó a su madre, pero en la ciudad se topa con los Mar, una comunidad que se reconoce descendiente de la criatura y que llevaba tiempo esperándola. Şahmaran apuesta por una fantasía de ritmo lento, más interesada en la atmósfera y en el peso de la profecía que en la acción. Umur Turagay dirige con una puesta en escena de cuento. Cerró su historia en una segunda temporada más breve.
Creada por Pınar Bulut y dirigida por Umur Turagay. Con Serenay Sarıkaya, Burak Deniz, Mustafa Uğurlu, Mahir Günşiray y Mert Ramazan Demir.
¿De quién huimos, mamá? (2023)
Género Thriller psicológico, drama. Nota FilmAffinity 5,1. Temporadas 1. Episodios 7.
Una madre y su hija llevan años sin domicilio fijo, encadenando hoteles y apartamentos de lujo para que nadie pueda seguirles el rastro. La niña ha crecido dentro de esa rutina sin entender del todo de qué escapan, y ¿De quién huimos, mamá? administra esa información con cuentagotas a lo largo de siete episodios. Funciona como thriller psicológico porque el peligro es casi siempre una posibilidad antes que una presencia, y porque la relación entre las dos protagonistas se sostiene en lo que no se dicen. Melisa Sözen construye una madre agotada y opaca sin pedir compasión. La brevedad juega a favor, ya que el mecanismo no tendría aire para estirarse mucho más.
Dirigida por Umut Aral y Gökçen Usta Çaylar. Con Melisa Sözen, Eylül Tumbar, Boran Kuzum y Ozan Dolunay.
Andropausia (2022)
Género Comedia, drama. Temporadas 1. Episodios 6.
Engin Günaydın escribe y protagoniza una comedia sobre el momento exacto en que un hombre de cincuenta años decide que su vida necesita una reforma integral. El personaje atraviesa lo que la serie bautiza como andropausia y reacciona con una sucesión de decisiones cuestionables que arrastran a todo su entorno. Andropausia se apoya en el humor incómodo y en un retrato bastante reconocible de la crisis de la mediana edad, repartido en seis episodios que rondan los cuarenta y cinco minutos. Los hermanos Taylan dirigen sin buscar la carcajada fácil. Dentro de las mejores series turcas en Netflix es una de las pocas propuestas de comedia adulta, un registro que el catálogo ha explorado menos que el drama.
Dirigida por Durul y Yağmur Taylan. Con Engin Günaydın, Tamer Karadağlı, Derya Karadaş, Gülçin Santırcıoğlu y Turgut Tunçalp.
Fiebre cerebral (2022)
Género Ciencia ficción, thriller. Nota FilmAffinity 5,4. Temporadas 1. Episodios 8.
La novela Sıcak Kafa, de Afşin Kum, imagina un virus que se transmite a través del habla y que convierte a quien lo contrae en un ser violento e incoherente. La adaptación traslada ese planteamiento a un futuro donde el contagio ya ha arrasado el país y un grupo reducido de personajes intenta sobrevivir en un pueblo. Fiebre cerebral aprovecha la idea central para construir una ciencia ficción de recursos limitados donde el silencio es la única defensa posible, y donde el trabajo con los personajes pesa tanto como la amenaza exterior. Mert Baykal firma la creación y comparte dirección con Umur Turagay. No pasó de su primera temporada de ocho episodios.
Creada por Mert Baykal. Con Osman Sonant, Şevket Çoruh, Hazal Subaşı, Hülya Köseoğlu y Haluk Bilginer.
Club Estambul (2023)
Género Drama, época. Nota FilmAffinity 6,4. Temporadas 2. Episodios 20.
Estambul, años cincuenta. Matilda sale de prisión y empieza a trabajar en un club nocturno de moda, donde intenta acercarse a la hija que no pudo criar y que hasta entonces desconocía su existencia. Club Estambul es un drama de época que usa el local y sus actuaciones en directo como escenario central, y que administra el reencuentro entre madre e hija con más calma que efectismo. La reconstrucción de vestuario y decorados queda por encima de la media del catálogo, y la música ocupa un lugar propio dentro del relato. Gökçe Bahadır sostiene el personaje con una contención poco habitual en el melodrama. La historia se completó en veinte episodios.
Creada por Zeynep Günay Tan. Con Gökçe Bahadır, Barış Arduç, Salih Bademci, Metin Akdülger y Fırat Tanış.
Fatma (2021)
Género Thriller, crimen. Nota FilmAffinity 5,7. Temporadas 1. Episodios 6.
Fatma limpia casas en Estambul y busca a un marido que ha desaparecido sin dejar rastro. Nadie de su entorno le presta demasiada atención, y esa invisibilidad acaba siendo su herramienta más útil cuando la búsqueda la mete en una espiral criminal que no había previsto. Fatma funciona porque no convierte a su protagonista en una vengadora, sino en una mujer que va tomando decisiones cada vez más difíciles de deshacer. Burcu Biricik construye el personaje casi sin diálogo, apoyada en la mirada y en el gesto contenido. Özgür Önürme firma la creación sobre una historia de Ahmet Vatan y resuelve el relato en seis episodios sin necesidad de continuación.
Creada por Özgür Önürme. Con Burcu Biricik, Uğur Yücel, Mehmet Yılmaz Ak, Hazal Türesan y Melis Sezen.
Nos conocimos en Estambul (2020)
Género Drama, coral. Nota FilmAffinity 7,2. Temporadas 1. Episodios 8.
Berkun Oya escribe y dirige la pieza más comentada del catálogo turco de la plataforma. Meryem trabaja como empleada doméstica en una familia conservadora de las afueras de Estambul y empieza a sufrir desmayos, así que acude a Peri, una psiquiatra cuya vida no se parece en nada a la suya. De esas sesiones nace un retrato de dos Turquías que se observan con desconfianza mutua, y esa tensión sociocultural es lo que distingue a Nos conocimos en Estambul dentro de las mejores series turcas en Netflix. El reparto coral está medido al detalle y Öykü Karayel sostiene el centro emocional del conjunto. Son ocho episodios autoconclusivos.
Creada por Berkun Oya. Con Öykü Karayel, Fatih Artman, Defne Kayalar, Funda Eryiğit y Tülin Özen.
Criatura (2023)
Género Fantástico, drama, terror. Nota FilmAffinity 4,6. Temporadas 1. Episodios 8.
Ziya estudia Medicina con la ambición de encontrar una cura para las enfermedades infecciosas, y su camino se cruza con el del doctor İhsan, a quien unos consideran un genio y otros un perturbado. Son las dos únicas personas capaces de entender la ambición del otro, y el experimento que emprenden juntos les va a costar caro. Criatura plantea una epopeya sobre la muerte y el más allá con ambientación histórica, escrita y dirigida por Çağan Irmak, uno de los nombres con más recorrido del cine turco. El aire de fábula gótica y el cuidado de los decorados pesan más que la velocidad del relato. Se resuelve en ocho episodios pensados para verse seguidos.
Creada por Çağan Irmak. Con Taner Ölmez, Erkan Kolçak Köstendil, Şifanur Gül y Bülent Şakrak.
Un fuerte aplauso (2024)
Género Comedia negra, drama. Temporadas 1. Episodios 6.
Seis episodios de menos de media hora bastan para completar esta comedia urbana que se ve en poco más de tres horas. Berkun Oya vuelve al catálogo con una propuesta alejada del tópico del melodrama turco, centrada en la vida cotidiana, el paso del tiempo, las relaciones y la paternidad. Un fuerte aplauso trabaja un humor negro que en ocasiones se vuelve surrealista, y quien busque una trama de giros va a encontrar más bien un retrato de la rutina y de las pequeñas cosas que la hacen soportable. Aslıhan Gürbüz y Fatih Artman llevan el peso de un reparto que se mueve en registros muy contenidos. Es la entrada más breve de la selección.
Creada por Berkun Oya. Con Aslıhan Gürbüz, Fatih Artman, Cihat Süvarioğlu, Serra Arıtürk y Rezdar Taştan.
La familia Uysal (2022)
Género Comedia negra, drama. Nota FilmAffinity 5,2. Temporadas 1. Episodios 8.
Oktay Uysal es arquitecto y ha montado una doble vida a espaldas de los suyos. Lo que no sospecha es que no es el único miembro de la familia que esconde algo, y ese reparto de secretos es el mecanismo que mueve La familia Uysal durante ocho episodios. El sarcasmo funciona como principal herramienta del guion, con un humor negro que exige atención porque casi nunca se explica a sí mismo. Onur Saylak dirige un reparto con nombres de peso del cine turco y deja que la incomodidad haga el trabajo que en otras comedias hace el chiste. No pasó de su primera temporada.
Dirigida por Onur Saylak. Con Öner Erkan, Uğur Yücel, Haluk Bilginer y Şebnem Bozoklu.
La vida y las películas de Erşan Kuneri (2022-2024)
Género Comedia. Temporadas 2. Episodios 16.
Cem Yılmaz escribe, dirige y protagoniza esta mirada irreverente a la trastienda del cine. Su personaje es una figura célebre del cine erótico que, tras revisar su propia obra, decide cambiar de registro y meterse en géneros como la ciencia ficción o la acción medieval, con resultados que rara vez acompañan a la ambición. La vida y las películas de Erşan Kuneri es una comedia de humor picante que reconstruye una industria de rodajes precarios y egos desmedidos. El protagonista no está pensado para caer bien y ahí reside buena parte de la gracia. Yılmaz reúne alrededor un elenco cómico amplio y suma dos temporadas de ocho episodios cada una.
Creada por Cem Yılmaz. Con Cem Yılmaz, Zafer Algöz, Ezgi Mola, Uraz Kaygılaroğlu y Çağlar Çorumlu.
Lobo (2018)
Género Acción, thriller. Nota FilmAffinity 5,2. Temporadas 1. Episodios 6.
Turquía, primavera de 2014. Con varios frentes abiertos en sus fronteras, el país afronta una de las mayores amenazas de su historia reciente y una unidad policial de operaciones especiales encadena misiones de alto riesgo por todo el territorio. Lobo reparte el foco entre esas intervenciones y el desgaste que producen en casa, con un tratamiento próximo al cine bélico. Es la propuesta más árida del conjunto y la que menos concesiones hace a quien llegue buscando romance, lo que también la convierte en una rareza dentro de las mejores series turcas en Netflix. Alper Çağlar firma la creación y el guion. Se quedó en seis episodios de una única temporada.
Creada por Alper Çağlar. Con Mesut Akusta, Ahu Türkpençe, Serkan Çayoğlu, Özge Gürel y Murat Arkın.
Enamorados anónimos (2025)
Género Comedia romántica, drama. Temporadas 1. Episodios 8.
Cem perdió la fe en el amor durante una infancia que preferiría no recordar y ha convertido ese desencanto en negocio, porque dirige un centro al que llama Hospital del Amor y donde atiende a quienes sufren por desamor. La llegada de Hazal, que sigue creyendo en aquello que él ha descartado, desmonta el método desde dentro. Enamorados anónimos es una comedia romántica con más drama del que aparenta, sostenida por el contraste entre dos formas opuestas de entender el vínculo amoroso. Halit Ergenç y Funda Eryiğit se reparten el juego con oficio. Umur Turagay dirige un guion de Başar Başaran y firma la incorporación más reciente de esta selección.
Dirigida por Umur Turagay. Con Halit Ergenç, Funda Eryiğit, Rıza Kocaoğlu, Cansel Elçin y Ecem Çalhan.
Asaf (2024)
Género Thriller, drama criminal. Temporadas 1. Episodios 6.
Özgür Önürme vuelve al thriller de gente común después de Fatma, otra vez con Ahmet Vatan en el guion. Aquí el protagonista es un conductor de valores firmes que atraviesa un mal momento tras separarse de su mujer y de su hijo, y un accidente de tráfico en apariencia menor lo pone en contacto con gente peligrosa. Asaf reconstruye en seis episodios el proceso por el que alguien corriente termina en situaciones extremas por acumulación de circunstancias, sin que medie una decisión propia. Cihangir Ceyhan sostiene el papel con una contención que evita el heroísmo, y la brevedad mantiene la tensión sin caídas de ritmo.
Creada por Özgür Önürme. Con Cihangir Ceyhan, Burçin Terzioğlu, Saadet Işıl Aksoy, Rıza Kocaoğlu y Uygar Özçelik.
¿Por dónde empezar tu maratón de series turcas en Netflix?
Si nunca has visto una producción turca y quieres comprobar si el registro te interesa, Nos conocimos en Estambul es la puerta más segura, porque funciona como drama coral cerrado en ocho episodios y no exige ningún compromiso largo. Cuando lo que buscas es un melodrama con recorrido y capítulos que se encadenan sin que te des cuenta, El sastre ofrece esa mecánica con un acabado visual muy cuidado.
Y si prefieres alejarte del drama, Andropausia demuestra que la comedia adulta también tiene su sitio entre las mejores series turcas en Netflix. Conviene tener en cuenta que buena parte de estas historias se cierra en una sola temporada, así que la duración del maratón depende bastante de por dónde decidas empezar.

articles.title: Don't put your phone in the fridge, if that wasn't already obvious
articles.text:
Summer heat can cause a lot of stress for some devices, especially if your phone is prone to overheating (like my Google Pixels). However, a common online cooling technique is damaging some devices.
Techspot noted that mobile repair shops in Europe have seen a steep rise in the number of people bringing in phones damaged by being put in the fridge to cool down.
Now, putting your overheating (or even just hot) phone in the fridge seems like a pretty easy solution. However, as Engadget pointed out, doing so could severely damage your device or even break it entirely.
To start, the main reason you shouldn’t do this is condensation. Essentially, when the phone is placed in a fridge, the hot air inside the device is cooled, which can cause condensation on sensitive parts. When it is taken out of the fridge and into warmer air after cooling, there is even a greater chance that the inside of the device will experience it again.
Also, if the difference between the outside temperature and the fridge temperature is extreme, there is a chance the refrigerator may be damaged by the rapid change. Known as thermal shock, this can shorten the device’s battery life, place excessive stress on the lithium battery, or even cause the screen to crack.
If you do want to cool your phone down without storing it with your leftovers, there are a few other ways that aren’t as extreme. These include removing your case, thermal pouches, and even portable cooling fans that can be attached via MagSafe.
Now, as someone who repairs devices as a hobby, condensation on devices is way more common during extreme temperature shifts (such as moving from overheating to the fridge), so don’t worry about it during temperature changes like in the winter.
If your phone does happen to overheat (which has happened to me plenty of times), the solution I usually use is to remove the case, set it down on a relatively cool surface (like a kitchen counter), and leave it be until it has cooled down to a safe temperature. Enjoy the time away from your phone.
Source: Engadget

articles.title: Sunbird relaunched its iMessage app for Android users after three years away
articles.text:
Sunbird Messaging is back on the Google Play Store, offering Android users blue bubble privileges in iMessage complete with reactions and high quality videos for $2.99 a month. Apple and Google have made cross platform messaging better in recent years with support for RCS, but Android users can still cause issues in iMessage group chats, like breaking reactions and replies.
Sunbird relaunched its iMessage app for Android users after three years away
The company claims it has addressed the security flaws that shut down its operation in 2023.
Android Authority reports that after Sunbird shut down nearly three years ago due to security issues, the company says its new setup addresses those, and that “Any message moving through our infrastructure is protected in transit and released once it’s delivered,” while media you send or receive is deleted “typically within 48 hours and never longer than 72.”
Your messages are encrypted on your phone before they leave it, encrypted in transit over certificate-pinned connections, and encrypted at rest on your device, using strong AES-256 encryption. On the final leg to an iPhone, your message is protected by Apple’s iMessage end-to-end encryption, which Sunbird never modifies, intercepts, or weakens.
Sunbird’s CEO Danny Mizrahi told Android Authority that “an independent security auditing firm tested its rebuilt Sunbird app,” and reported “no critical vulnerabilities.” Mizrahi also added that, “When a user connects iMessage, their Apple ID password is used once to set up the session and then destroyed. We do not store the password, and we do not keep an authentication token that would let us sign in as them later.”
You can also access Google Messages and SMS from Sunbird, and support for integrating WhatsApp and Facebook Messenger is coming later this year, along with an AI assistant that can summarize chats and draft replies.

articles.title: AI makes weather prediction better. Can WindBorne make it lucrative? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The new deep learning techniques behind LLMs have also given us weather simulations that can run on laptops instead of supercomputers, changing meteorology. But the bigger task for AI may be making it easier for people and organizations to put those forecasts to work.
WindBorne Systems, a startup that collects data with the world’s longest-flying weather balloons and feeds it into a powerful forecasting model, has raised a $37 million Series B round to take on that challenge, CEO John Dean told TechCrunch.
The new round was co-led by Khosla Ventures and Galvanize, with additional investments from TransLink Capital, Lux Capital, and previous investors, and values the company after this round of funding at $250 million.
Founded in 2019, WindBorne started with a plan to acquire a novel set of weather data with its low-cost weather sensors and endurance balloons. The development of AI weather forecasting models in the last four years has allowed them to make their own forecasts, something that wasn’t previously possible for most private companies because of the cost of the supercomputers previously required to simulate the atmosphere.
Today, the company has 20 launch sites around the world and about 600 balloons in the air at any given time, collecting data in hard-to-reach areas, like the eye of a typhoon. Now, the company is beginning to deploy aerial sensor packages that can fall into the ocean and continue collecting measurements as floating buoys.
The proprietary data set generated by this “planetary nervous system,” as Dean likes to call it, creates a moat for their weather model, which also ingests data sets generated by government weather agencies around the world.
“We demonstrated that when you add balloons to the forecast, you get more accurate forecasts, and the value per data point is much stronger than satellites,” Dean said. “We’ve also been growing revenue while we’re doing that, so that de-risked the demand signal to VCs.”
The company’s main customers today are government agencies. The U.S. National Weather Service purchases the company’s data, while the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy are paying WindBorne through research partnerships, including an effort to develop forecasting models that can be run onboard ships that may have intermittent connections to the rest of the world.
What’s next is commercial business — right now, that’s mainly focused on investment funds that use weather data to predict commodity prices and other business outcomes. Besides spending on compute and an effort to replace the balloon network’s satellite communications with a mesh radio network, this round will let WindBorne build out its go-to-market team to expand its customer base in the private sector.
That’s not always easy. In the last decade, a variety of startups have tried to scale up sensing businesses like earth observing satellite networks, but found it difficult to break through to the private sector because extracting value from that data requires experience and established workflows. Most turn to government agencies that are used to employing that data already.
Private weather forecast companies do exist, but make most of their money repackaging or refining government forecasts for the news media, specialized needs like plane de-icing and ship routing, or the above-mentioned speculators. That, however, may change as AI tools makes data crunching more efficient.
Saloni Multani, a partner at Galvanize who co-led the round, said that the private weather market has been limited because “integrating weather forecasts into broader business decision-making has traditionally been expensive and difficult. We think AI changes that equation. Better forecasts make the effort worthwhile, and AI makes it much easier to connect those forecasts to the decisions businesses are trying to make.”

articles.title: 16GB GPUs and 8-core CPUs officially become the most popular configs on Steam — Latest hardware survey shows modern gaming's growing hunger for more resources
articles.text:
16GB GPUs and 8-core CPUs officially become the most popular configs on Steam — Latest hardware survey shows modern gaming's growing hunger for more resources
The new era is officially here, ordained by the Lord Gaben himself.
Wirth's law dictates that software becomes slower more rapidly than hardware gets faster. That logic can explain why games today look mostly the same as they did a decade ago, yet require a lot more resources to run comfortably. That sentiment is now reflected in Steam's latest hardware survey as well, where 8-core CPUs have overtaken 6-core CPUs for the first time ever, and GPUs with 16GB of VRAM have become the most common on the platform.
The results for July 2026 show that 16GB GPUs now represent 25.9% of all Steam users, just edging out 8GB GPUs that sit at 25.32% adoption. In June, 16GB GPUs were at 24.50%, so they gained 1.4 points in a month, while 8GB GPUs lost 0.32 points in the same time. This is the first month in the storefront's history where 8GB of VRAM is no longer considered enough, closing the book on this debate in a rather definitive way. Keep in mind that these numbers combine all Steam instances across Windows, Linux, and Mac.
When it comes to processors, the need to move away from 6-core chips hasn't really been of concern since they're still enough for gaming. It was not long ago that Intel was refreshing the same quad-core CPUs year after year until AMD's resurgence pushed the industry out of stagnation. This is evident by the fact that 4-core CPUs still enjoy a 13.2% share of the pie. But today, it's clear that the shift has begun as Steam's most recent data shows 27.85% of the userbase is rocking 8-core CPUs, while 27.52% have 6-core CPUs.
Once again, it's the first time this precedent has shifted as 8-core chips became 0.32% more popular this month compared to last, the most of any config, while 6-core chips lost 0.12% of their adoption. The extreme popularity of X3D chips for gaming is partly responsible, since the 5800X3D, then the 7800X3D, and now, the 9800X3D, all feature 8 cores and 16 threads. Intel's hybrid architecture makes it so that pretty much none of its midrange or high-end chips have exactly 8 cores (though many have 8 P-cores).
The obsolescence of 6-core CPUs and 8GB GPUs is not a sudden event; we've been witnessing this decline since at least last year, when their numbers first started to dwindle. Sales figures from across the world, multiple times, have shown how customers heavily prefer to buy 16GB versions of the same GPUs that also have an 8GB model. Such a small memory pool is simply not enough for modern games, especially since they've begun relying on ray tracing as a requirement now.
"What Andy gives, Bill takes away" is a niche adage in the tech space that referred to Microsoft's bloatware outpacing hardware advancements made by Intel back in the 90s. It still holds true today, but it's better combined with May's Law — the idea that the abundance of silicon will make developers lazy, such that they'll stop optimizing their code to its fullest potential. Of course, this is a bit ironic considering we're in a component crisis at the moment, where soaring memory and storage prices are now coming to bite back said developers.
The consumers are not stuck with the debt of years of inefficiency. If you still have an 8GB GPU today, like the 5060 Ti, there's a high chance you won't be able to play upcoming modern games smoothly, even if the core itself remains perfectly capable. Anyhow, the Steam Hardware Survey doesn't represent the entire market, obviously, but it's a good indication of mainstream trends. They show that the RTX 3060 is still the most popular current-gen card in the world, while the RTX 5070 is climbing the charts fast. AMD and Intel are basically honorable mentions on this list.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Hassam Nasir is a die-hard hardware enthusiast with years of experience as a tech editor and writer, focusing on detailed CPU comparisons and general hardware news. When he’s not working, you’ll find him bending tubes for his ever-evolving custom water-loop gaming rig or benchmarking the latest CPUs and GPUs just for fun.
