articles.title: Disney gives TikTok creators official access to Marvel, Star Wars, and Pixar characters
articles.text:
Disney is introducing fan-created TikTok content to its Disney Plus app in its latest attempt to break into short-form creator videos. The Walt Disney Company announced today that it’s partnering with TikTok to bring “an expansive collection of thoughtfully curated Disney-centric fan-created content” to the Verts video feed it launched on Disney Plus earlier this year, providing creators with access to assets from “hundreds” of movies and TV shows.
Disney gives TikTok creators official access to Marvel, Star Wars, and Pixar characters
Disney Plus will host ‘thoughtfully curated’ fan-made videos starting in the US.
The partnership will be piloted in the US “in the coming months,” according to Disney, with plans to launch in other markets later. Videos from TikTok creators who opt-in to the program will be hosted on both the TikTok and Disney Plus platforms, and will feature a host of scenes and characters from Disney’s brands, including Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, and more. Disney says the jointly-run creator program will also grant certain perks to participating TikTok creators, including increased visibility, exclusive event access, and career development pathways.
Disney was planning a similar partnership with OpenAI that would have allowed the AI provider’s now defunct Sora video generator to train on and replicate protected Disney IP, in exchange for hosting Sora-made videos on Disney Plus. There’s nothing in Disney’s new partnership with TikTok that specifically excludes AI tools, but we’ve reached out to clarify.

articles.title: Zürich-based Exclaim Robotics exits stealth with €4.29 million to build robots for AI data centre maintenance | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Exclaim Robotics, a Zürich-based startup building robots to maintain AI data centres, has exited stealth mode with a €4.29 million ($4.95 million) pre-Seed round co-led by Founderful and Playfair.
The company is building autonomous mobile robots that perform routine repair and maintenance work inside AI data centres.
“The speed of innovation in data centre infrastructure is reminiscent of the space race: power density is pushing the whole industry to the edge of the laws of physics. Liquid cooling, 800V DC across the whole facility, possibly superconducting bus bars cooled with liquid nitrogen. Maintaining that by hand gets more dangerous every year, and that’s the part robots should take,” said Helen Oleynikova, CEO and Founder of Exclaim Robotics.
Founded in 2026 by Oleynikova, who spent 15 years working in robotics across Willow Garage, Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and ETH Zürich, and holds a PhD from ETH Zürich in mapping and planning for cluttered, unstructured environments. She co-created nvblox, the 3D mapping and collision-avoidance library now shipped in NVIDIA Isaac ROS and used by robotics teams worldwide.
She is joined by founding engineer Patrick Pfreundschuh, who holds a PhD from ETH Zürich, created the BIEVR-LIO LiDAR-inertial odometry system, and was part of the winning team at the DARPA Subterranean Challenge. Two more founding engineers will be joining the company in 2027.
The company states that the next generation of AI data centres will distribute power at 800 volts DC directly inside the rack. At that voltage, opening a rack carries arc-flash risk, and ordinary maintenance, such as replacing a failed drive or reseating an optical transceiver, becomes hazardous work.
The shift comes amid a rapid buildout of AI data centre capacity, which is outpacing the supply of trained technicians, says Exclaim Robotics.
Almost everything in a modern data centre is managed remotely: provisioning, scheduling, failover, and networking. The physical layer is the exception. When hardware fails, someone still has to walk to the rack.
The robot being built by Exclaim has to navigate the data hall on its own, position itself at a rack, and work the front face from the floor to the top rail, without any changes to the building.
The company is starting with the highest-volume break-fix tasks, which are replacing and cleaning optics and SFPs, copper network cabling, and drive replacement.
Exclaim notes that its approach is to train in simulation first, where a robot can practise a task far more times than is possible on real hardware, and then repeat the work on real racks with real sensors until it is reliable enough to trust.
“The harder problem is the environment rather than the motion: racks are dense with cabling, and a robot has to understand what it is looking at before it can safely touch anything. Where its confidence in a task is low, it will hand off to a remote operator rather than attempt it,” the startup mentioned.
“AI data centres are scaling faster than anyone can staff or safely maintain them, and the 800V transition will change everything about how that infrastructure gets run. Helen and her team from ETH Zürich, NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Google are the people to solve it. We backed Exclaim because Helen is exactly the founder you want when a hard problem becomes urgent,” said Antonia Albert, Principal at Founderful.
The company plans to use this capital to build its first prototypes, acquire robotics hardware, and grow the engineering team. It is currently hiring robotics and hardware engineers in Zürich.
Exclaim’s longer-term goal is to apply the same capability wherever infrastructure maintenance is hazardous, remote, or hard to reach, with high-voltage and energy infrastructure as the next target.

articles.title: Bis zu 50 Prozent mehr: Warum Motherboards wohl bald deutlich teurer werden
articles.text:
Bis zu 50 Prozent mehr: Warum auch Motherboards wohl bald deutlich teurer werden
Der KI-Boom sorgt aktuell für eine Speicherkrise. RAM-Riegel und Speicherchips werden immer teurer und Expert:innen schlagen Alarm, dass dieser Zustand auch noch Jahre anhalten und dabei einige Unternehmen in den finanziellen Ruin treiben könnte. Obwohl das Problem für RAM und Speicher noch nicht behoben ist, bahnt sich schon die nächste Krise an.
Werden Motherboards bald deutlich teurer?
Das geht auf einen Post in den Board Channels zurück, einem chinesischen Forum für Tech-Lieferketten. Die Webseite Videocardz hat dort Zugang bekommen und ist dabei auf einen Beitrag gestoßen, der über Preisanstiege für Motherboards berichtet. Der Post trägt den Titel: „Taiwanesische Motherboard-Hersteller warnen vor einem geplanten Preisanstieg im dritten Quartal.“
Demnach stehen Motherboard-Hersteller in Taiwan aktuell drei großen Herausforderungen gegenüber. Zunächst sinken die Verkaufszahlen, weil das Interesse am PC-Eigenbau und an Bastelprojekten stetig sinkt. Dazu kommt, dass die Preise für Motherboards in den vergangenen Monaten stagnieren, aber gleichzeitig die Kosten für die Herstellung wachsen. Die Preise für Kupfer, Kondensatoren und Chips sind so signifikant angestiegen, dass davon auszugehen ist, dass einige Motherboard-Hersteller 2026 deutlich weniger Umsatz machen werden.
Aufgrund dieser Informationen kann laut den Insider:innen davon ausgegangen werden, dass taiwanesische Motherboard-Hersteller wie Asus, Gigabyte und MSI im dritten Quartal 2026 eine Preisanpassung anstreben. Aktuellen Schätzungen nach könnte der Preis je nach Motherboard um bis zu 50 Prozent ansteigen. Dadurch sollen die Herstellungskosten gedeckt werden.
Wer gegen Ende des Jahres einen neuen PC bauen möchte, dürfte also nicht nur bei RAM und Speicher drauflegen, sondern muss offenbar auch für das Motherboard tiefer in die Tasche greifen. Wie Videocardz betont, gibt es aber aktuell keine großen Anreize, ein Upgrade von einem funktionierenden Motherboard durchzuführen. Das liegt daran, dass viele neue Motherboards im Vergleich zu älteren Modellen nur neue Speicher- und RAM-Generationen unterstützen. Da diese sowieso so teuer sind, dass sich der Griff dazu kaum lohnt, muss auch nicht zwingend das neueste Motherboard erworben werden.

articles.title: Apple India FY26 revenue grows 20% to near Rs 1 lakh Cr
articles.text:
Apple India FY26 revenue grows 20% to near Rs 1 lakh Cr
According to Counterpoint research, Apple's iPhone shipments for FY26 grew to 14 million units, up 24% year-on-year.
Apple's India revenue grew by over 20% in FY26 to near Rs 1 lakh crore, with iPhone shipments growing 24% year-on-year, according to industry sources.
Apple India had posted consolidated revenue of around Rs 79,000 crore in the financial year 2025.
"Apple's revenue in India has crossed $10 billion due to record shipments of iPhone in FY26. In Indian rupee terms, it was somewhere close to the Rs 1 lakh crore revenue mark," said a source aware of the development.
Apple has been posting record performance in India over the last several quarters.
According to research by market research and analysis firm Counterpoint, Apple's iPhone shipments for FY26 grew to 14 million units, up 24% year-on-year.
The iPhone accounts for the majority of Apple's revenue in India.
Neil Shah, Co-founder and VP for Research at Counterpoint, said India has emerged as a cornerstone growth market for Apple, driven by rapid iPhone adoption as mature smartphone users trade up to premium devices.
"Over the last few years, Apple has systematically built momentum through an expanded retail footprint, localised manufacturing, and flexible financing options. This strategy is now creating a powerful flywheel effect for its brand as the expanding iPhone user base adopts broader ecosystem offerings spanning Macs to services such as Apple Music," he said.
IDC India analyst Navkendar Singh said India was again a standout for Apple in the recently reported quarter, setting another revenue record with double-digit growth.
"On a still-modest share of the world's second-largest smartphone market, that signals a long runway, powered by first-time buyers, wider retail and financing access, and roughly a quarter of iPhones now assembled locally.
"The near-term will test this—Apple has flagged significant supply constraints in the next few quarters, and a global memory-cost crunch is pushing prices up. Prices for iPhones will see an increase in the next few weeks; however, demand should absorb it," Singh said.

articles.title: Clip Pro : prix cassé et fiche technique musclée, tout savoir sur les écouteurs open-ear de CMF
articles.text:
Clip Pro : prix cassé et fiche technique musclée, tout savoir sur les écouteurs open-ear de CMF
CMF fait son entrée sur le marché des écouteurs clipsables avec les Clip Pro. Ce premier modèle mise sur un format ouvert favorisant le confort, une autonomie annoncée de 10 h et une connectivité avancée, le tout à un tarif accessible au regard de la concurrence.
Si Nothing a été contrainte d’annuler la sortie de ses prochains smartphones CMF en raison de la flambée des prix de la RAM, elle entend bien accélérer dans le développement d’accessoires. Elle fait ainsi son entrée sur le marché en pleine expansion des écouteurs ouverts clipsables avec les CMF Clip Pro. Ces derniers s’adressent aussi bien aux utilisateurs souhaitant rester attentifs à leur environnement qu’à ceux pour qui les embouts en silicone sont inconfortables.
CMF Clip Pro
Une conception à clip standard, pensée pour allier confort et maintien
Composés d’une coque circulaire abritant la partie acoustique et d’un module arrière intégrant la batterie, reliés par un arceau venant se fixer sur le lobe de l’oreille, les Clip Pro ne réinventent pas le format.
L’arceau adopte une structure en titane, un matériau à mémoire de forme annoncé comme capable de supporter des milliers de manipulations sans perdre ses propriétés mécaniques. Celui-ci est recouvert d’un revêtement en TPU présenté comme doux pour la peau, tandis que ses dimensions auraient été étudiées pour convenir à la majorité des morphologies, afin de concilier confort et maintien.
Davantage préconisés pour le quotidien que pour le sport, les Clip Pro bénéficient d’une simple certification IP54 pour une résistance minimale aux intempéries.
Ouverture acoustique inclinée et molette cliquable sur le boîtier
La partie acoustique prend la forme d’une boule ronde et compacte, dans l’esprit des Huawei FreeClip 2. L’objectif est de limiter la sensation de présence dans le creux de l’oreille tout en conservant un volume suffisant pour intégrer une architecture sonore soignée. L’ouverture acoustique est légèrement inclinée afin de conserver une bonne directivité lorsque les écouteurs sont légèrement orientés vers le bas, une position permettant de rapprocher la chambre acoustique du conduit auditif.
Le boîtier de charge reprend la molette cliquable déjà présente sur plusieurs modèles d’écouteurs CMF. Entièrement personnalisable depuis l’application, elle permet de gérer différentes fonctions au choix parmi la lecture, le réglage du volume, l’assistant vocal, les appels et l'activation/désactivation des microphones.
Si les écouteurs peuvent être placés dans le boîtier dans n’importe quel sens, la permutation automatique des canaux n’est pas de mise. Chaque écouteur dispose donc d’indications droite/gauche afin d’être positionné correctement, une concession par rapport aux modèles premium de Huawei ou Shokz.
Transducteurs de 10,8 mm et algorithme maison de renforcement des basses
Sur le plan acoustique, les Clip Pro misent sur un unique transducteur de 10,8 mm doté d’une conception à double aimant censée renforcer l’assise dans les basses. Un point délicat sur les écouteurs ouverts, naturellement en déficit dans les très basses fréquences.
Selon CMF, combinant du TPU et du LCP, leur membrane permettrait d’obtenir "un son moins agressif que les diaphragmes utilisant des matériaux plus rigides", tout en réduisant la distorsion à volume élevé. La marque indique également avoir développé un algorithme capable de compenser activement le manque d’extension dans le bas du spectre. Les Clip Pro intègrent par ailleurs une fonction destinée à limiter les fuites sonores inhérentes au format. Celle-ci semble agir en atténuant certaines fréquences médiums et aiguës. Accessible depuis l’app Nothing X, celle-ci semble agir en atténuant certaines fréquences médiums et aiguës.
Concernant les appels, CMF promet une captation claire en environnement bruyant grâce à deux microphones par écouteur associés à un algorithme de réduction des bruits ambiants. Le premier est dédié à la captation de la voix, tandis que le second détecte le vent.
Connectivité Hi-Res, boutons physiques, autonomie de 10 h, etc.
Comme les autres écouteurs Nothing et CMF, les Clip Pro embarquent une puce Bluetooth 5.4 compatible avec le codec LDAC. Cette compatibilité Hi-Res peut sembler superflue sur des écouteurs ouverts, dépourvus d’isolation acoustique, mais elle reste un avantage appréciable sur cette gamme de prix. Les écouteurs prennent également en charge la connexion multipoint, l’appairage rapide sur Android via Fast Pair et Swift Pair, ainsi qu’un mode basse latence accessible depuis l’app.
À l’image du modèle de Bose, mais contrairement aux itérations Shokz et Huawei, les commandes des Clip Pro reposent exclusivement sur des boutons physiques. Placé à l’extrémité supérieure de la partie arrière des écouteurs, ce bouton permet de contrôler la lecture grâce à des pressions simples ou multiples, ainsi que le volume via des appuis prolongés sur l’écouteur gauche ou droit. Une approche un peu passéiste, mais qui tend à limiter les commandes accidentelles.
Côté autonomie, les CMF Clip Pro promettent jusqu’à 10 h d’écoute sur une seule charge, auxquelles s’ajoutent 22 h 30 min d’autonomie supplémentaire grâce au boîtier de charge. Une endurance solide compte tenu de leur positionnement tarifaire, même si les Shokz OpenDots 2 annoncent jusqu’à 40 h d’autonomie totale avec leur boîtier. CMF précise également que 10 min de recharge suffisent à récupérer jusqu’à 4 h de lecture.
Disponibles dès aujourd’hui dans des coloris noir, blanc et orange, les CMF Clip Pro sont proposés au tarif de 79 £ (prix en euros à venir). À ce tarif, ils se montrent particulièrement abordables pour des écouteurs clipsables, la majorité des modèles sérieux du marché étant actuellement proposés au-delà de 130 €. Au regard des caractéristiques annoncées, les Clip Pro pourraient donc devenir une nouvelle référence en matière de rapport prix-performances sur ce segment.

articles.title: Apple va rendre le copier-coller de l’iPhone compatible avec Windows 11
articles.text:
Vous pourrez bientôt copier-coller du contenu entre votre iPhone et votre PC sous Windows 11. Apple travaille en effet officiellement sur une solution visant rendre le presse-papiers d’iOS compatible avec Windows.
Cette nouvelle fonctionnalité n’est pas le fruit de la volonté d’Apple. Il s’agit en réalité d’une demande opérée par Microsoft, dans le cadre de la réglementation européenne (DMA).
« Le copier-coller entre appareils est une fonctionnalité de productivité très demandée et l’expérience entre appareils la plus appréciée par les utilisateurs qui travaillent sur plusieurs appareils. Apple prend en charge le copier-coller entre appareils entre iOS et macOS via une intégration système propriétaire. Cependant, les plateformes tierces ne peuvent pas offrir une expérience comparable avec leurs propres appareils en raison des restrictions sur l’accès au presse-papiers sur iOS. » a indiqué la firme de Redmond dans le motif de sa demande.
L’objectif est donc d’obliger Apple à proposer aux utilisateurs de Windows une expérience de copier-coller plus fluide, à l’image de ce que la firme de Cupertino propose déjà entre iOS et macOS.
Apple va synchroniser le presse-papiers d’iOS avec Windows 11
La synchronisation du presse-papier d’iOS avec un ordinateur, cela existe déjà, mais de manière très limitée. Apple ne l’autorise en effet qu’entre un iPhone et un Mac. Et, sécurité oblige, les restrictions en place dans iOS empêchent toute initiative des développeurs tiers de proposer une solution pour synchroniser le presse-papiers d’iOS avec Windows.
En effet, une application ne peut pour l’heure accéder au contenu du presse-papiers d’iOS que lorsqu’elle est ouverte au premier plan. L’utilisateur doit par ailleurs accorder son autorisation avant que l’application puisse accéder à celui-ci à chaque fois. Surtout, Apple ne propose aucune API permettant d’accéder de manière persistante en arrière-plan au presse-papier pour le synchroniser.
Pour que les utilisateurs sous Windows ne soient pas lésés, Microsoft a donc demandé à ce qu’Apple planche sur une solution technique autorisant la synchronisation du presse-papier avec Windows. La demande, repérée par MacRumors, a été faite en mars dernier sur la page dédiée aux demandes d’interopérabilité des fonctions d’iOS dans l’UE.
Microsoft a d’ailleurs détaillé ce que permettrait l’interopérabilité de cette fonctionnalité sur Windows pour les utilisateurs de l’UE :
- Copier du texte ou tout autre contenu pris en charge sur leur iPhone et collez-le directement sur leur PC Windows, et vice versa.
- Effectuer des flux de travail de productivité courants sans avoir besoin de mettre en avant une application ou de prendre des mesures répétées explicites pour lancer un transfert.
- Découvrir la synchronisation du presse-papiers comme une fonctionnalité légère et continue plutôt que comme une opération manuelle pilotée par une application.
Le copier-coller de l’iPhone sur votre PC dès la fin 2027
Courant juin, Apple a validé le passage à une phase de mise en œuvre technique. L’interopérabilité du presse-papiers d’iOS avec Windows reposera ainsi sur plusieurs éléments. Apple compte introduire un nouveau mécanisme permettant de créer une extension pour partager et importer des éléments du presse-papiers avec des « accessoires appairés », comme une PC connecté à votre iPhone en Bluetooth.
Pour y arriver, le système s’appuiera sur plusieurs frameworks (Accessory Notifications, Accessory Live Activities et Accessory Transport Extension) et proposera un système de consentement simplifié. L’utilisateur n’aura ainsi qu’à donner son autorisation d’accès au presse-papiers de l’iPhone qu’une seule fois à l’appairage de son iPhone avec son PC Windows 11.
Si cette nouvelle possibilité est à l’heure actuelle toujours en cours de développement, elle pourrait être déployée dès l’an prochain. La fin du développement serait a priori prévue pour l’automne 2027, avec un lancement en bêta auprès des développeurs, puis au grand public, d’ici à la fin de l’année 2027, avec iOS 28 donc.
Cette nouvelle fonction, bien que pratique, pourrait néanmoins fragiliser la sécurité des données des utilisateurs. Car accorder un accès au presse-papiers de l’iPhone à Windows pourrait se transformer en porte ouverte pour l’interception de données potentiellement sensibles, comme des identifiants et des mots de passe.

articles.title: Over 400 NPM Packages Infected in ChainDrop Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
More than 2,200 malicious versions of 440 packages were published to the NPM registry as part of a fresh Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain attack.
Dubbed ChainDrop, the campaign started with 11 malware carriers in the keyv and cacheable namespaces, after their maintainer’s GitHub account was compromised.
Combined, the infected packages have over 500 million weekly downloads. They are widely used across the ecosystem and their poisoning led to 433 additional packages being infected.
Similar to previous Mini Shai-Hulud attacks, the infected packages executed malicious code during installation, dropping an information stealer with self-propagation functionality.
On the infected machines, the malware targets all the secrets it can find, encrypts them, and then exfiltrates the data either to a dynamic HTTPS endpoint or to attacker-created public GitHub repositories that have the ‘Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again’ description.
“Once executed, the malware searches developer workstations and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environments for NPM, GitHub, cloud, and infrastructure credentials. It uses recovered identities to authenticate to NPM, GitHub, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Kubernetes, and HashiCorp Vault, enabling it to enumerate packages, repositories, workflow secrets, cloud parameters, and secret-store values,” Microsoft explains.
Additionally, the malware uses the stolen NPM credentials to publish poisoned versions of every package it can reach on the infected machine, and leverages compromised GitHub credentials and GitHub Actions to infect more repositories for credential theft, JFrog says.
“After obtaining an NPM publishing token, it enumerates packages available to the compromised identity, downloads their latest tarballs, inserts the malware and setup loader, adds a preinstall hook, increments the patch version, and republishes the modified packages. The malware can also use stolen GitHub credentials to inject Claude and Visual Studio Code configuration files into repositories, establishing persistence and creating an additional developer-to-developer infection path,” Microsoft notes.
Because the malware republished many historical versions of the compromised packages, the total number of malicious package iterations observed on August 4 reached 2,212 in under four hours, StepSecurity says.
All infected package versions contained a preinstall dropper designed to download the legitimate Bun JavaScript runtime alongside 710 KB of obfuscated second-stage code representing the actual malware.
An evolved descendant of the Shai-Hulud 2.0 worm, the malware uses an Ethereum blockchain for command-and-control (C&C), a technique called EtherHiding.
The worm also installs a host-level dead-man’s switch: after achieving persistence on macOS and Linux, it polls the GitHub API using the victim’s stolen GitHub token every 60 seconds, and deletes its state and exits if the token stops working. It also self-clears after 24 hours, Socket notes.
NPM developers who installed any of the infected package versions should consider their machines compromised. They are advised to remove the malware, rebuild CI runners and build machines, revoke and rotate potentially compromised credentials, and audit their GitHub repositories for anomalous activity.
“Isolate affected systems. Preserve package tarballs, npm logs, CI logs, GitHub audit logs, and runner images before cleanup. You will need them to bound the exposure window,” JFrog recommends.

articles.title: Alguien está haciendo negocio con la ola de calor europea: China y sus trenes llenos de aires acondicionados
articles.text:
La ola de calor europea tiene una lectura evidente, la de las temperaturas, los avisos meteorológicos y las ciudades intentando funcionar bajo un calor cada vez menos excepcional. Pero también tiene otra menos visible y muy reveladora: alguien tiene que fabricar, vender y mover todo ese frío que Europa empieza a necesitar. Lo que hemos visto este verano es que esa oportunidad no la están aprovechando solo las tiendas locales ni los instaladores. También la está aprovechando China, con sus grandes fabricantes de aire acondicionado y una red ferroviaria capaz de recortar tiempos entre China y Europa.
El negocio del frío. El dato lo dejó el planificador económico chino en una rueda de prensa celebrada el 28 de julio: según recogió Yicai de esa comparecencia, fabricantes como Midea y Gree habían trasladado parte de sus reposiciones europeas del transporte marítimo al tren China-Europa. El cambio permite reducir el ciclo logístico de unos 40 días por barco a alrededor de 15 por ferrocarril. No hablamos, por tanto, de una ruta improvisada, sino de una respuesta comercial a una demanda que no puede esperar al calendario habitual del comercio marítimo.
No es una línea. Los trenes China-Europa no son un convoy aislado que sale de una ciudad china y llega siempre al mismo destino europeo, sino una red de servicios ferroviarios de contenedores que Pekín agrupa bajo la marca China-Europe Railway Express. El planificador económico chino la presenta como una pieza emblemática de la Franja y la Ruta, con una marca unificada desde 2016 y conexiones entre ciudades chinas y mercados europeos.
Europa tiene calor. La demanda no aparece en el vacío: Copernicus situó junio de 2026 como el más cálido registrado en Europa occidental y la Organización Meteorológica Mundial describió récords y episodios extremos en varios países. En España, a finales de julio, hablábamos de la llegada de una cuarta ola de calor del verano, con temperaturas que podían superar los 42 ºC en algunas zonas. Francia ofrece otra pista de mercado: Le Monde daba cuenta de que las ventas de climatizadores habían subido un 61% en mayo. No es solo meteorología, es consumo acelerado.
Los vagones ya salen. Las cifras locales chinas ayudan a bajar la historia a tierra. El Gobierno de Wuhan detalla que en junio sus servicios ferroviarios hacia Europa y Asia Central transportaron un 88,24% más de aires acondicionados y componentes que un año antes, con mercancía dirigida a Polonia, Alemania e Italia. Zhengzhou aporta otra fotografía: un tren con destino Duisburgo salió con 55 TEU, 17 de ellos cargados con unos 4.000 aparatos. Y desde la Gran Bahía Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao se comunicaron más de 100.000 unidades completas enviadas por tren entre abril y junio, además de componentes clave.
El tiempo importa. El barco seguirá siendo la opción habitual para mover grandes volúmenes, pero esta historia va de otra cosa: de llegar antes de que la demanda empiece a enfriarse. Las fuentes locales chinas hablan de trayectos ferroviarios de 15 a 20 días frente a más de 40 por mar, una diferencia que cambia el sentido de la reposición. Si un comercio europeo se queda sin aparatos en pleno pico de demanda, recibirlos a mitad del verano no es lo mismo que recibirlos cuando el episodio extremo ya ha pasado.
China gana dos veces. Por un lado, fabricantes como Midea llegan a un mercado donde las compras se han acelerado y donde todavía hay mucho margen: Reuters, citando a la Agencia Internacional de la Energía, situaba la penetración del aire acondicionado en Europa en torno al 20%. La compañía china ya había dicho al mismo medio que su PortaSplit se había agotado en algunos canales, con subidas en ventas y envíos en mercados como Alemania, España y Francia.

articles.title: C'est la fin de Google Assistant sur Android - Numerama
articles.text:
La retraite de Google Assistant est désormais programmée. Dans un mail envoyé à ses utilisateurs et repéré par Android Authority, Google annonce qu’il commencera à retirer son assistant vocal historique à partir du 4 septembre 2026.
Tous les smartphones ne basculeront pas vers Gemini le même jour, mais Google prévient que Google Assistant ne sera plus disponible une fois la transition déclenchée. Google permet depuis 2024 d’utiliser Gemini comme assistant par défaut en France, mais laissait encore les utilisateurs revenir à Google Assistant. Cette porte de sortie va disparaître.
À partir du 4 septembre, Gemini devient obligatoire sur Android
Après la migration, prononcer « OK Google » ou maintenir le bouton d’alimentation de son smartphone lancera Gemini.
Les exigences matérielles sont modestes : l’application Gemini fonctionne sur les smartphones et tablettes équipés d’au moins 2 Go de mémoire vive et d’Android 9. En France, la plupart des appareils encore utilisés devraient donc être concernés. Les produits trop anciens, les régions où Gemini n’est pas proposé et certains comptes non compatibles, pourront conserver Google Assistant.
Sur le papier, Gemini marque une vraie évolution pour les utilisateurs d’Android. L’assistant s’appuie sur les grands modèles de langage de Google et peut comprendre des demandes approximatives, maintenir le contexte d’une conversation, analyser ce qui apparaît à l’écran et interagir avec des services comme Gmail, Google Maps, YouTube ou Google Agenda, mais remplacer Google Assistant pose aussi quelques enjeux. L’ancien logiciel était limité… mais plus rapide pour passer un appel, lancer un minuteur, envoyer un message ou contrôler un appareil connecté. Google a dû reconstruire progressivement ces fonctions dans Gemini, ce qui explique ce remplacement tardif.
Les montres Wear OS, les écouteurs et Android Auto vont aussi perdre Google Assistant
La date du 4 septembre ne concerne pas seulement les smartphones. Quand Gemini devient l’assistant d’un téléphone, il remplace également Google Assistant sur plusieurs appareils jumelés :
- Les tablettes Android compatibles ;
- Les montres sous Wear OS ;
- Les écouteurs et casques compatibles avec Gemini ;
- Les véhicules utilisant Android Auto depuis un smartphone.
Dans ces différents cas, l’utilisateur ne pourra plus revenir à Google Assistant après la migration. Google avait annoncé dès mai 2025 l’arrivée de Gemini sur ses voitures, ses montres et ses téléviseurs, mais sans donner de date précise pour la disparition de son ancien assistant.
Une exception subsiste pour les voitures équipées de Google built-in, dans lesquelles Android est directement intégré. Google précise que Google Assistant continuera d’y fonctionner après le 4 septembre. Leur migration vers Gemini interviendra plus tard.
Google Assistant ne disparaîtra pas partout le 4 septembre
Les enceintes Google Home et Google Nest, les écrans connectés et les téléviseurs Google TV suivent, eux aussi, leur propre calendrier. Gemini for Home est disponible en accès anticipé depuis avril 2026, mais le remplacement est encore loin d’être total. Google Assistant survivra donc encore quelque temps sur les enceintes avant, très certainement, de laisser sa place à Gemini de manière définitive.

articles.title: Microsoft a forcé Apple à combler un manque que les utilisateurs Windows subissent depuis des années
articles.text:
Sous la pression du DMA européen, Apple a accepté de développer le copier-coller entre iPhone et PC Windows. Une fonction que les utilisateurs Android ont depuis des années, et qui n’arrivera pas avant l’automne 2027.
Microsoft a beau posséder le meilleur outil de connexion Android-PC avec Phone Link, ses propres utilisateurs Windows couplés à un iPhone se heurtent à un mur : impossible de copier-coller entre les deux appareils sans bricoler une application tierce au premier plan. C’est cette lacune, banale à résoudre côté Android, qu’Apple vient enfin d’accepter de combler. Pas de sa propre initiative : la demande de Microsoft, déposée le 25 mars 2026 dans le cadre des obligations d’interopérabilité du DMA européen, a contraint Cupertino à ouvrir un chantier qu’elle avait jusqu’ici soigneusement évité. Selon 9to5Mac, Apple a confirmé le 26 juin son intention de développer une solution.
Le presse-papiers iPhone-Windows, un an de retard sur ce qu’Android fait déjà
Android bénéficie depuis plusieurs années d’une synchronisation du presse-papiers avec Windows via Phone Link et SwiftKey. Côté iPhone, rien d’équivalent n’existait : chaque partage exigeait une application ouverte en premier plan et une validation manuelle à chaque copie. Microsoft a donc formalisé sa demande en trois points précis : copier sur iPhone, coller sur Windows (et vice-versa) sans manipulation répétée, sans application au premier plan, comme une capacité légère et continue plutôt qu’un transfert déclenché à la main.
Apple dispose pourtant d’Universal Clipboard, qui synchronise le presse-papiers en temps réel entre Mac, iPhone et iPad. L’argument de Microsoft est imparable : pourquoi les utilisateurs Windows seraient-ils exclus d’une fonctionnalité que les possesseurs de Mac ont depuis des années ? La firme de Redmond a d’ailleurs pris soin de préciser que son intention n’est pas de reproduire l’expérience Apple, mais d’offrir « un niveau de base de productivité multiplateforme que les utilisateurs attendent déjà ». Difficile de lui donner tort.
iOS 28 en ligne de mire, mais uniquement pour l’Europe dans un premier temps
L’implémentation technique qu’Apple a retenue s’appuie sur AccessorySetupKit et Accessory Transport Extension, les mêmes briques que celles utilisées pour d’autres demandes DMA récentes. Concrètement : une extension déclenchée dès qu’un élément est copié sur l’iPhone, qui transfère automatiquement le contenu vers le PC Windows appairé. L’utilisateur devra accorder l’autorisation une seule fois par appareil Windows, ce qui reste raisonnable. Apple qualifie le projet d’« effort d'ingénierie significatif » et vise une bêta développeur à l’automne 2027, avant une disponibilité publique qui coïnciderait vraisemblablement avec iOS 28.
Le calendrier soulève une question plus gênante que le délai lui-même : la fonction pourrait rester cantonnée à l’Union européenne, puisqu’elle découle directement du processus DMA. Ce n’est pas une certitude, Apple ayant parfois généralisé ce type d’ouvertures à l’échelle mondiale, comme ce fut le cas pour l’émulation. Mais l’exemple de Galaxy Connect de Samsung sur Windows 11 rappelle que la concurrence n’attend pas les régulateurs pour avancer sur ce terrain.
Un an et demi de développement pour une fonction que SwiftKey propose en quelques clics côté Android : le contraste dit beaucoup sur la réticence historique d’Apple à ouvrir son écosystème en dehors de ses propres appareils. La vraie inconnue reste la portée géographique du déploiement. Si Apple limite la synchronisation à l’Europe, les utilisateurs américains devront soit patienter soit espérer une pression réglementaire similaire de la FTC. Est-ce que Microsoft ira jusque-là pour ses utilisateurs Windows ?

articles.title: Crean un sensor blando de luz para monitorear la actividad del corazón y el cerebro
articles.text:
Durante décadas, estudiar la actividad eléctrica del corazón o del cerebro exigió colocar en el cuerpo dispositivos fabricados con materiales rígidos —como el silicio y los metales— que frecuentemente dañan los tejidos blandos o provocan el rechazo del implante.
Pero ahora, un equipo de ingenieros biomédicos de la Universidad de Nueva Gales del Sur (UNSW), en Australia, presentó un sensor óptico completamente flexible, bautizado como optrode, que convierte las señales eléctricas del organismo en impulsos de luz sin necesidad de cables ni electrónica local. El dispositivo, probado en animales, registró una tasa de viabilidad celular del 98,4%, lo que sugiere que el cuerpo lo tolera bien.
PUBLICIDAD
Enfermedades como la epilepsia refractaria, las arritmias cardíacas o los accidentes cerebrovasculares exigen vigilancia continua de señales eléctricas muy débiles: un paciente puede necesitar un implante que registre durante semanas la actividad de su corteza cerebral para que los médicos localicen con exactitud el foco de las convulsiones, información imprescindible antes de considerar una cirugía.
Los dispositivos disponibles, sin embargo, generan interferencias eléctricas, producen calor cerca de los tejidos y pierden precisión a medida que se miniaturizan. Los hallazgos se publicaron en la revista npj Flexible Electronics.
PUBLICIDAD
Un material que imita al cuerpo humano
Para entender la novedad del optrode, se puede recurrir a una analogía: los implantes tradicionales son como introducir una varilla de metal dentro de una esponja mojada. La dureza del material daña la esponja con el tiempo.
El nuevo sensor, en cambio, está fabricado con polímeros blandos de alto rendimiento —materiales plásticos especialmente diseñados para interactuar sin riesgo con los tejidos del cuerpo— que imitan la suavidad y la flexibilidad de los órganos internos.
PUBLICIDAD
Uno de esos polímeros conserva su capacidad conductora incluso después de ser doblado 10.000 veces, un requisito indispensable para cualquier implante sometido al movimiento constante del corazón o del pulmón.
En la capa central del dispositivo se ubica una lámina de cristales líquidos —la misma clase de tecnología que forma las imágenes en los televisores y monitores modernos— con una sensibilidad capaz de detectar variaciones de señal a niveles de submillivoltio.
PUBLICIDAD
Para dar una idea de la escala: un millivoltio equivale a la milésima parte de un volt, la unidad eléctrica que alimenta una pila de linterna. Las señales del cerebro y del corazón son aún más débiles que eso.
“Los implantes bioelectrónicos son dispositivos que pueden colocarse en el cuerpo para monitorear señales eléctricas de órganos como el corazón y el cerebro. Ayudan a los médicos a rastrear cambios y patrones en la salud de una persona a corto y largo plazo”, afirmó la doctora Reem Almasri, primera autora del trabajo e investigadora de la Escuela de Ingeniería Biomédica de UNSW, según el comunicado de prensa de la institución.
PUBLICIDAD
Luz en lugar de electricidad
El mecanismo central del optrode se basa en un proceso llamado transducción pasiva: cuando llega una señal eléctrica —por ejemplo, la que emite el corazón al latir—, los cristales líquidos reorientan físicamente su posición en función de la intensidad de esa señal.
Ese cambio de orientación altera la forma en que la luz los atraviesa, y esa variación lumínica se convierte en la información medible. El sensor no genera electricidad propia ni interfiere con la actividad natural del órgano.
PUBLICIDAD
“Diseñamos este sistema para que los cristales orienten su ángulo dependiendo de la amplitud de la señal aplicada, por ejemplo, una señal cerebral. Mediante señales de luz, mide el porcentaje de cambio y lo convierte en salidas ópticas cuantificables”, explicó Almasri.
La ausencia de amplificadores y cables metálicos en el sitio de contacto con el tejido resuelve otro de los problemas clásicos de los electrodos convencionales. Los aparatos del entorno —equipos médicos, luminaria, otros dispositivos— generan campos electromagnéticos que contaminan las lecturas biológicas; al operar con luz, el nuevo sensor queda blindado frente a ese tipo de interferencias.
PUBLICIDAD
“Los amplificadores pueden ayudar a reducir la interferencia eléctrica y mejorar la calidad de la señal en el sitio. Sin embargo, suelen ser voluminosos y pueden generar calor alrededor del tejido circundante, lo que potencialmente limita el rendimiento del sistema“, señaló la investigadora.
Tamaño microscópico, señal intacta
Una de las ventajas más notorias del nuevo dispositivo es su capacidad para reducir su tamaño a escala microscópica sin perder calidad de lectura. Los electrodos convencionales enfrentan una paradoja técnica: cuanto más pequeños se fabrican, más difícil resulta separar la señal biológica del ruido de fondo eléctrico. El optrode sortea esa limitación al funcionar en el dominio de la luz y no en el de la electricidad.
PUBLICIDAD
“En nuestra tecnología, podemos reducir el sensor a decenas de micrones —aproximadamente la mitad del ancho de un cabello humano— sin perder calidad de señal ni introducir ruido eléctrico adicional“, según la Universidad de Nueva Gales del Sur. Un micrón equivale a una milésima parte de un milímetro: a esa escala, el dispositivo podría apoyarse sobre un único tipo de célula sin afectar a las vecinas.
Las pruebas de compatibilidad biológica también arrojaron datos positivos. El equipo evaluó el comportamiento del sensor en cultivos celulares —muestras de células mantenidas vivas en laboratorio— y no encontró signos de toxicidad ni contaminación.
“Nuestras pruebas in vitro mostraron que el optrode no afectó el crecimiento ni la viabilidad celular en comparación con los controles de silicio, que se usan ampliamente en los dispositivos actuales de biomonitoreo”, afirmó Almasri.
Aunque los resultados en animales validan las capacidades del sensor, los investigadores identifican nuevos estudios in vivo —en organismos vivos, a diferencia de los cultivos de laboratorio— como el paso inmediato para mejorar la resolución de las lecturas.
El equipo también apunta a ampliar el rango de frecuencias del dispositivo: “Queremos expandir el ancho de banda de la señal más allá de los 10 kilohertz para capturar el disparo de neuronas individuales”, detalló Almasri.
Un kilohertz equivale a mil ciclos por segundo; aumentar ese umbral permitiría registrar la actividad de cada neurona por separado, algo que los sistemas actuales no pueden hacer con precisión.
Más allá del corazón y el cerebro, la tecnología tiene proyección hacia otras zonas del organismo: el intestino, los músculos o incluso células individuales. “También hay una oportunidad para mejorar la alineación de los cristales líquidos. Si aumentamos la sensibilidad del dispositivo, podríamos detectar señales a nivel de micrón“, señaló Almasri.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Renault R5 : la gamme s'allège aujourd'hui pour préparer une mise à jour majeure cet automne
articles.text:
Sur le configurateur français, la série spéciale Roland-Garros de la R5 électrique n’apparaît plus en gris mat. Le changement a été repéré par des passionnés sur le forum Worldscoop. Un détail, sauf qu’il ne vient pas seul : Renault raccourcit en ce moment plusieurs de ses menus de personnalisation.
La R5 électrique cartonne. Lancée début 2024, la citadine s’est écoulée à plus de 100 000 exemplaires en un peu plus d’un an et figure parmi les voitures électriques les plus vendues d’Europe. Elle sort de l’usine Renault de Douai, dans le Nord, où elle partage la même ligne d’assemblage que les Mégane E-Tech et Scénic E-Tech. C’est justement là que se joue ce ménage, selon Forococheselectricos : on simplifie l’offre avant une refonte prévue pour septembre-octobre.
Moins d’options maintenant, plus de nouveautés à l’automne
Le tri ne touche pas que la R5. Sur le Trafic, l’utilitaire comme la version particulière, les jantes en aluminium disparaissent de la liste des options. Même logique sur les gammes Kangoo. En coupant des variantes, Renault réduit le nombre de références à gérer en usine et sur les chaînes d’approvisionnement, ce qui simplifie la production et fait baisser les coûts.
Il est possible que la mise à jour apporte de nouvelles couleurs, dont un rouge. Le Rouge Carmin n’est pas produit à Douai, contrairement au Rouge Flamme, qui pourrait facilement y être appliqué parce qu’il équipe aussi la Mégane et le Scénic assemblés sur le même site.
Peindre une carrosserie dans une teinte partagée par plusieurs modèles revient moins cher que d’entretenir une couleur dédiée à une seule voiture. Moins de teintes exclusives entraîne moins de contraintes logistiques.
Rien d’inquiétant pour l’acheteur. Ce genre de nettoyage précède presque toujours un restylage, le temps d’écouler les configurations existantes. Le vrai intérêt se trouve dans ce qui arrive derrière : de nouvelles couleurs, des batteries LFP moins chères, des moteurs plus efficaces et surtout davantage d’autonomie, aujourd’hui plafonnée autour de 400 kilomètres. Renault fabrique déjà ces cellules en France, un point qui compte pour le bonus et le prix final.
Attention toutefois au calendrier. La refonte de l’automne portera surtout sur les couleurs et la gamme d’options. Les batteries LFP moins chères et les nouveaux moteurs plus efficaces, eux, sont annoncés pour plus tard : Marianne Bataillon, en charge des moteurs et batteries chez Renault, a indiqué à Autocar qu’ils arriveraient fin 2026 ou début 2027.
Si vous lorgnez une R5 aujourd’hui, l’entrée de gamme Five à 24 990 euros reste dans le catalogue. Mais pour qui n’est pas pressé, attendre la version de l’automne a du sens : plus de rayon d’action pour un budget qui devrait rester contenu. Sur le papier, la logique tient ; les tarifs de la nouvelle gamme diront si le client y gagne vraiment.

articles.title: LexisNexis opens customer innovation lab driven by AI to change the future of legal work - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
LexisNexis opens customer innovation lab driven by AI to change the future of legal work
LexisNexis Legal & Professional, a division of RELX plc, today announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City, which will deliver a new model for how legal artificial intelligence gets built.
The company said the shift is designed to bring AI directly into the grasp of legal professionals. Instead of building AI solutions and then dropping them in the customer’s lap for feedback, the lab will bring legal workers, LexisNexis engineers, and AI technology together in a collaboration.
LexisNexis framed this not as “vibe consulting,” but as augmenting customer discovery and development with access to artificial intelligence and professional expertise. The human- and customer-centric approach is designed to bring real solutions together that can quickly turn into tested prototypes in hours or days and production-ready software within weeks.
“Our vision is to empower customers with world-leading, purpose-built and trusted legal AI,” said Chief Technology Officer Greg Dickason. “The Customer Innovation Lab changes who’s in the room when legal AI gets built. Customers help originate and shape what we build from day one.”
The lab brings together legal professionals from law firms, corporate legal departments, judiciary and academia to speak to pain points and challenges within legal practice. Engineers then work with them to build AI solutions in real time. The prototypes are then designed and tested the same day against the real-world problems they were built to solve, bringing results and working models to legal professionals to identify seams and issues.
Projects only advance when a solution displays proven quality, accuracy and security alongside immediate customer feedback, iterating on actual needs.
According to Thomson Reuters, lawyers spend around 40% to 60% of their time drafting and reviewing documents; LexisNexis said it has independently verified this pattern with customers who told the company the complex nature of legal work dominates legal drafting, falling into personalization, tonality, strategic understanding and subject matter expertise. The paperwork is eating the work with paper.
LexisNexis said the Lab is building and prototyping AI and agentic drafting to help adapt a firm or organization’s drafting style, precedents and playbooks into one place. The same solutions assist with risk flagging and redline suggestions using a customer’s own standards, allowing them to carry context across vast related document sets using document-aware editing tools designed to work within a specific legal expertise.
Technology collaborators, including OpenAI Group PBC and Amazon Web Services Inc., have participated alongside customers and LexisNexis teams.
The company said the Lab is already shipping solutions developed from customer ideation and engineering expertise. Solutions include LexisNexis-developed legal AI models, purpose-built for legal work using authoritative legal content; an advanced customer-managed Protégé Vault, which allows customers to securely store and analyze documents, videos, images, audio files and other material together within the legal process; and Secure Protégé Workrooms, which provides a space for team collaboration augmented with AI assistants built with carefully curated permissions and access controls.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Project BRIDGE targets 90,000km fibre network by 2030
articles.text:
Nigeria’s ambition to become Africa’s digital economy powerhouse now rests on a company that has yet to be legally incorporated.
The federal government expects to register the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) that will oversee Project BRIDGE by July 31, laying the legal foundation for one of Nigeria’s largest digital infrastructure projects. The incorporation date will not mark a public launch or the start of operations. Rather, it is the point at which the project company will formally come into existence, according to Jumoke Akande, Project Lead at the Project Implementation Unit, Federal Ministry of Communication, Innovation, and Digital Economy.
The company’s final legal name has not been disclosed. World Bank project documents currently refer to it as the “Project Company,” “Project BRIDGE SPV,” or simply the “SPV.”
“The final legal name of the SPV is confidential and has not yet been publicly disclosed,” Akande told TechCabal on Sunday. “For now, it is referred to in the relevant documents as the “Project Company”, the “Project BRIDGE SPV” or simply the “SPV”.”
Once established, the SPV will be responsible for mobilising private capital, coordinating construction across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, and overseeing the deployment of at least 90,000 kilometres of climate-resilient fibre optic networks by September 2030.
That leaves a little room for delay.
Before large-scale construction can begin, the SPV must complete investor selection, achieve financial close, finalise engineering designs, conduct route surveys, secure permits and negotiate right-of-way agreements. Physical deployment is expected to begin in 2027, leaving roughly three and a half years to build a network that would dramatically expand Nigeria’s digital backbone.
If successful, Project BRIDGE would increase Nigeria’s fibre backbone to about 120,000 kilometres, extend connectivity to more than 770 local government areas, and connect thousands of schools, hospitals and other public institutions.
The project is designed around a wholesale, open-access model rather than a new retail telecommunications operator. The SPV will provide infrastructure that mobile network operators, Internet service providers and enterprise customers can use on non-discriminatory terms.
That distinction is important. Nigeria is not simply building another fibre network. It is attempting to create shared infrastructure that lowers the cost of connectivity while allowing multiple operators to expand services without each having to build its own backbone.
The World Bank is providing $500 million through the International Development Association, while another $1.1 billion is expected to come from private and other commercial financing. Additional development finance institutions are also participating, including the African Development Bank with $200 million, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development with $100 million, and BADEA with another $100 million.
“All fundraising figures published are subject to a detailed model built by the transaction advisers which will provide guidance specifically on the total amount of funding required for the project,” Akande said. “This is not publicly available. The $2 billion figure used in some earlier descriptions was a broader or rounded preliminary estimate, while US$1.6 billion is the financing envelope formally appraised and approved by the World Bank.”
The next phase, therefore, is as much about financial engineering as it is about laying fibre.
More than 30 local and international companies expressed interest during the government’s market-sounding and prequalification process, according to project documents. Incorporation of the SPV is expected to allow the government to move towards final investment agreements and construction contracts.
The proposed ownership structure gives control to private investors. They are expected to hold between 51% and 75% of the SPV, while the federal government will retain a minority stake of between 25% and 49%. An independent board and private-sector management are intended to limit political interference while giving the company the commercial flexibility required to execute the project.
Attracting investors, however, may prove easier than delivering the network. The construction schedule is ambitious. Project plans call for about 17,500 kilometres of fibre to be deployed in the first year, followed by 25,000 kilometres in each of 2028 and 2029. A further 22,500 kilometres must then be completed during the final nine months of 2030.
At its peak, crews across the country would need to install roughly 80 to 90 kilometres of fibre every day.
To manage the scale of the rollout, Nigeria plans to divide the project into six engineering, procurement and construction zones operating simultaneously. Contractors in each zone would each be responsible for deploying hundreds of kilometres of fibre every month.
The challenge will not end with trenching and laying cable. Project milestones also include activating wholesale interconnection hubs, connecting public institutions, reducing wholesale bandwidth prices, expanding connectivity to more than 400 local government headquarters, and building redundant network routes to minimise the impact of cable cuts.
The government expects the infrastructure to increase broadband users from about 92 million to 150 million by 2030, reduce wholesale bandwidth prices by 17%, raise fixed broadband speeds to 50 Mbps and connect more than 59,000 public institutions to high-speed Internet.
The programme also includes digital literacy training for 37,000 Nigerians, with women expected to account for 60% of participants.
Those targets explain why the project matters beyond the telecom industry.
Nigeria’s digital economy increasingly depends on the availability and affordability of connectivity. A larger national fibre backbone could enable operators and Internet service providers to expand into areas where deployment is currently uneconomic, while greater wholesale competition could reduce the cost of capacity.
But the economics of the project remain exposed to the same pressures confronting much of Nigeria’s infrastructure sector.
The World Bank has classified the programme’s overall risk as substantial, citing governance, procurement and institutional capacity challenges, alongside macroeconomic pressures such as inflation and foreign-exchange volatility.
Right-of-way approvals present another potential bottleneck. Although more than 11 states have agreed to waive right-of-way fees, according to the ministry, inconsistent local charges and administrative delays could still slow construction.
Protecting the network once it is built poses an equally significant challenge. Project BRIDGE will need to secure a steady supply of fibre and ducting while deploying thousands of kilometres of cable across difficult terrain, from remote northern communities to riverine areas in the south. The scale of the threat is already evident. Telcom operators recorded a record 155,397 fibre cuts in April and May 2026 alone—74,276 in April and 79,121 in May. More than 54,000 of those incidents were attributed to vandalism, underscoring the challenge of safeguarding the very infrastructure the project is intended to expand.
The threat persists despite Nigeria’s Critical National Information Infrastructure (CNII) Order, gazetted by the President on June 25, 2024, to protect critical digital and technological assets and ensure their uninterrupted operation. For Project BRIDGE, however, the rest of the test will be translating that legal framework into effective protection for tens of thousands of kilometres of fibre.
If successful, the open-access model could reduce duplicated fibre infrastructure by allowing multiple operators to share one backbone, lowering costs and expanding broadband to underserved areas. But the model depends on the SPV securing capital, operating commercially and building quickly. Its July incorporation is therefore only the starting point; execution will require investors, contractors and governments to coordinate thousands of kilometres of construction.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: AI agents can create database sprawl issues. YugabyteDB’s solution is more agents!
articles.text:
AI agents can create database sprawl issues. YugabyteDB’s solution is more agents!
The next database scaling problem may not be how big a database gets, but how many databases an enterprise suddenly has to run.
That’s the inspiration behind YugabyteDB AMP, or Agentic Multitenant Postgres, a new serverless PostgreSQL tier designed for a world in which companies could be running hundreds or thousands of AI agents, each generating its own data layer demands. For Yugabyte, that means rethinking what scale looks like.
Karthik Ranganathan, co-founder and co-CEO of Yugabyte, tells The New Stack, “The dimension of scale is shifting. It’s not just large databases; it’s also a proliferation of databases.”
“The dimension of scale is shifting. It’s not just large databases; it’s also a proliferation of databases.”
YugabyteDB AMP extends Yugabyte’s reach to the smaller end of that spectrum, while maintaining the distributed architecture the company has traditionally built for large, mission-critical workloads. It uses serverless multitenancy and what Yugabyte calls Enhanced Colocation to pack hundreds of workloads onto shared infrastructure, while giving each agent an isolated PostgreSQL database.
The economics make sense for fleets of databases, including those that underpin AI agents. An experimental agent might hammer its database for a few minutes, and then the database might sit untouched for days or even be destroyed after the task was completed. YugabyteDB AMP scales to zero when that workload is idle and charges by CPU minute when it is running.
Yugabyte is also seeing another problem will appear alongside all those databases: the need for someone (or something) to manage them.
Four agents walk into a database
YugabyteDB AMP ships with four custom built-in agents: Architect, Voyager, Perf Advisor, and Nexus.
Yes, Yugabyte’s answer to the infrastructure needed by AI agents is, in part, more AI agents.
YugabyteDB Architect handles database creation and provisioning. A company might have rules about where development and staging databases live, how much compute they receive, or whether a particular workload needs to span multiple regions. Architect retains that organizational context and applies it when an agent asks for infrastructure.
“There’s a lot of context that we build up as humans that needs to get harnessed by this agent.”
“It needs to have context about your organization, about your specific group, about the details of your application,” Ranganathan says. “There’s a lot of context that we build up as humans that needs to get harnessed by this agent.”
YugabyteDB Voyager handles migration and modernization. It’s designed to bring existing databases into the fold. Voyager works out sizing and scaling requirements, as well as any changes needed to move workloads from other databases onto PostgreSQL.
Then there’s YugabyteDB Perf Advisor, which looks after databases once they are running. It can investigate an outage or performance problem, search information about the database and its environment, and attempt to determine the root cause. Yugabyte also wants it to catch problems earlier, including warning developers when a query is likely to cause trouble before it reaches production.
Finally, YugabyteDB Nexus handles the ecosystem around the database: connecting it to warehouses, data streams, key management systems, and other external infrastructure.
Ranganathan says those four agents are just the starting point: “These were the four that it ships with today, with the substrate to be able to do more.”
The more interesting part is what sits between them. The agents share context about the organization and maintain a record of why they made particular decisions. If somebody later asks, as Ranganathan puts it, “What the hell was that?” Yugabyte wants you to be able to reconstruct what happened.
“This is what the person said. This is what your context said. This is what I inferred. This is what I ended up doing.”
“This is what the person said. This is what your context said. This is what I inferred. This is what I ended up doing,” he says, describing the decision traces Meko maintains around agent actions for YugabyteDB AMP.
Giving agents the keys, with conditions
There is an obvious catch to letting AI agents provision, tune, and otherwise fiddle with databases: sometimes they do stupid things.
Ranganathan describes the autonomy YugabyteDB AMP gives its agents as a “guarded amount of freedom,” with the level of control depending on the environment.
A disposable development database might be configured so the agent can get on with the job without repeatedly asking permission. A production system holding financial information would be treated very differently.
“There would be a dry run mode. It’ll tell you what it wants to do,” he says. “So you can always say, ‘Ask me permission before you do something, and ask me permission, especially if the operations fall in this category.’”
He doesn’t pretend those controls make mistakes impossible. “It’s how you configure and use the thing that matters.”
What happens if the prototype actually works?
There is another problem YugabyteDB is trying to support: successful experiments.
Teams can start an AI project on a small serverless database because it’s cheap and convenient. Auto-scaling down to fractional vCPUs keeps those early-stage deployments inexpensive, while database branching lets developers spin up isolated copies to test new ideas, agents, or features without affecting production.
If the application becomes heavily used or business-critical, however, the infrastructure it started with may no longer be enough. YugabyteDB AMP is designed so that developers don’t have to switch databases at that point.
As the workload grows, YugabyteDB can move to YSQL, its distributed PostgreSQL layer, adding horizontal write scaling, multi-master replication and geo-distribution. Yugabyte says this doesn’t require an application rewrite or a conventional database migration, and that the agent continues to connect in the same way.
It will also give companies some choice about where all this runs. YugabyteDB AMP can operate inside a customer’s own cloud, connected back to YugabyteDB’s control plane. Yugabyte calls the latter BYOC, or bring your own cloud. Future deployment options will include an unsharded PostgreSQL managed service.
The idea is that metering, management, and learnings can still flow through the control plane while the customer’s data remains in its own environment. “We still want it to be secure enough and for customers to feel secure enough to run it wherever their data is,” Ranganathan says.
How Yugabyte manages its own database sprawl
YugabyteDB AMP is still in its early stages and isn’t broadly available yet. Yugabyte is using it internally and has opened it up to a small number of selected partners, with wider availability expected soon.
The company is already running agents internally for coding, support, and go-to-market work. Its support agent is called Hagen, while Growth Vector handles go-to-market tasks. YugabyteDB AMP is also being used for development, and Ranganathan says Yugabyte is starting to move other internal databases onto it.
“We’re trying to consolidate all our databases as well,” he says. “Same problem, right?”
Whether most enterprises end up with enormous fleets of agents with enormous fleets of databases remains an open question. The agent market is still moving quickly enough that today’s indispensable architecture can become tomorrow’s abandoned experiment.
Yugabyte doesn’t need every agent to survive for YugabyteDB AMP’s premise to make sense, though. Quite the opposite. Its bet is that companies will create lots of them; most will spend time doing nothing; some will disappear; and a small number will unexpectedly become important.
If that happens, the database problem becomes less about finding somewhere to put one enormous workload and more about keeping track of many little ones.
And if humans can’t reasonably manage them all, Yugabyte already has four agents volunteering for the job.

articles.title: I tested the Fanxiang PS2000W and found a solid portable SSD that's another victim of the rising memory prices
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Fanxiang PS2000W portable SSD ticks most of the boxes with the possible exception of hardware encryption. However, the price of flash-based external SSDs isn’t sustainable at current levels, including this drive.
Pros
- +Lightweight
- +Durable
- +Cable for USB-A and USB-C
Cons
- -Recent 100% price increase
- -Needs USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 for full performance
- -Lacks hardware encryption
Why you can trust TechRadar
Fanxiang PS2000W: 30-second review
Fanxiang is a Chinese storage brand, most commonly known as Shenzhen Fanxiang Information Technology. The company grew out of a team with a decade of prior experience in storage design, firmware, and product sales, and they've built their range around four main product lines: solid-state drives, mobile storage, memory modules, and storage cards.
It’s been making external SSD storage for about five years, with a wide range of devices and specifications.
The PS2000W appeared in 2025, and delivers capacities from 500Mb to 4TB in a slim aluminium case. It comes with a soft carry pouch and a cable that has an integrated adapter for both USB-A and USB-C connections.
The quoted performance is 2000MB/s reads, and 1800MB/s writes, but that assumes you have a USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 port, and that’s not a common standard.
More realistically, a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port will achieve a little over 1000 MB/s reads, and 950 MB/s writes with either a USB-C or USB-A connection.
For those wanting faster transfers, you either need a system with the rare USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 port, or choose a different drive that supports the USB4 standard, like the Fanxiang PS3000 portable SSD.
However, that option costs $350 for the 1TB model, which is substantially more than the $150 the PS2000W is typically priced at for that capacity.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The problem the PS2000W doesn’t address is that this drive is double the price it was only eight months ago, and unless you have a system that can make the most of its enhanced performance, there are cheaper alternatives. In fact, if you have a spare NVMe drive, then buying an external enclosure for USB4 is probably a better choice.
Not the best portable SSD, or the worst, but sadly impacted by the outrageous cost of flash memory in 2026.
Fanxiang PS2000W: Pricing and availability
- How much does it cost? Starts from $90
- When is it out? Available now
- Where can you get it? Sold through online retailers and also directly from Fanxiang.
The Fanxiang PS2000W portable SSD comes in capacities starting at 500 GB, doubling each step to include 1TB, 2TB, and 4TB drives.
Directly from the maker, these are priced at $112.99, $203.99, $379.99 and $495.99 for the largest capacity. That pricing makes the 4TB the best value, and the 500MB the worst.
But the maker prices aren’t especially good, and I was able to find it much cheaper on Amazon. On Amazon.com in the US, the 500MB model is only $89.99, the 1TB model is $149.99, and the 4TB model is $419.99. There wasn’t a price for the 2TB version.
UK pricing via Amazon.co.uk is £64.60, £119.99, £169.99, and £319.99, and Amazon EU sites are €94.99, €139.99, €229.99, and €379.99, respectively.
For those curious, the UK is the cheapest place to buy this hardware, followed by the EU, and the most expensive is the USA.
While officially Crucial has exited the retail market, its equivalent product, the X10, is still available from many retailers. At $207 for the 1TB option, and $299.99 for the 2TB option, the X10 is slightly more expensive. But it is rated as water-resistant, and while there isn’t a 500GB model, there are 6TB and 8TB options.
A cheaper option with the same spec is the PNY RP60, but the 1TB model is still $10 more than the PS2000W.
But many of the familiar brands are more expensive, such as the SanDisk Extreme Pro V2, Samsung T9, Kingston XS2000 and LaCie Rugged Mini. Western Digital has its My Passport SSD, but it’s the same price as the PS2000W, but only offers half the performance.
Those looking for a cheaper option should consider the $82 Orico S20 with 512GB storage.
It’s tempting to look at the pricing of the PS2000W and see it as a good deal, when it’s far from that.
Price tracking the 1TB model: it was $149.99 at the time of writing; it was $75.99 in November of 2025. That’s nearly a 100% markup.
Now, I should say that Fanxiang doesn’t control the price of Flash memory, which has spiked since AI companies and speculators decided to buy all of it. But in good conscience, I can’t recommend people spend this sort of money on devices that cost half as much a year ago.
- Value: 3 / 5
Fanxiang PS2000W: Specs
| Model | Fanxiang PS2000W | 
| Interface | USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 (20Gbps) | 
| Sequential read | Up to 2050MB/s | 
| Sequential write | Up to 1800MB/s | 
| Flash type | TLC 3D NAND | 
| Capacities | 500GB, 1TB, 2TB | 
| Dimensions | 8.5cm x 5cm x 0.8cm | 
| Weight | Approximately 45g | 
| Build | Aluminium alloy unibody | 
| Cables included | USB Type C to C, plus Type C to A adapter | 
| Compatibility | Windows, Mac, Android, PS5/PS4, iPhone 15 and later via USB-C | 
| Warranty | 5 years | 
Fanxiang PS2000W: Design
- Aluminium enclosure
- Dual USB standards cable
Some brands, and you know the names, will try to make their external SSDs and HDDs as cheaply as possible, typically by using mostly plastic construction.
Thankfully, Fanxiang didn’t go down that path with the PS2000W, and this device appears to be entirely made of metal. And, based on its relatively low weight, it uses aluminium.
The package is a simple lozenge shape with curved sides and flattened ends, measuring 85mm long by 50mm wide and less than a centimetre thick.
Out of the box, it comes with a 30cm USB-C to USB-C cable that has a USB-A adapter permanently attached. The drive and cable fit neatly into a soft drawstring bag, also provided, making for a neat and easily pocketable solution.
The review model was a 2TB capacity drive, which translated into 1863GiB of usable space, and it connects to the host device using USAP (Serial ATA).
To achieve the best performance, it requires a USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 port, but the drive is backwards compatible with USB 3.2 Gen 2, Gen 1, and even USB 2.0. However, as you move down the USB interface pecking order, the expected speed decreases.
As for features, this drive is basic. It supports S.M.A.R.T. NCQ, TRIM and GPL, but it doesn’t offer hardware encryption like on the Kingston XS2000 or the Crucial X10 Pro.
There are also no software tools included, though you can download a utility for SSD management from the Fanxiang website. I didn’t notice any means to update the installed firmware, or any firmware releases.
To be blunt, this is a basic USB SSD with a Gen 2x2 interface, but otherwise it’s unremarkable. And therefore, if you don’t have that interface, there appears to be no compelling reason why you would choose this one over another brand.
- Design: 3.5 / 5
Fanxiang PS2000W: Performance
- Needs USB 3.2 Gen 2x2
- Performs within quoted specification
| Fanxiang PS2000W Benchmark |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Bench | Test | USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 | USB 3.2 Gen 2 | 
| CrystalDiskMark 9.03 | Default Read | 2002MB/s | 1041MB/s | 
| Row 2 - Cell 0 | Default Write | 1853MB/s | 948MB/S | 
| Row 3 - Cell 0 | Real World Read | 1336MB/s | 993MB/s | 
| Row 4 - Cell 0 | Real World Write | 1219MB/s | 912MB/s | 
| AJA System Test 64GB | Read | 1804MB/s | 971MB/s | 
| Row 6 - Cell 0 | Write | 1645MB/s | 891MB/s | 
| AS SSD | Read | 1771MB/s | 971MB/s | 
| Row 8 - Cell 0 | Write | 1496MB/s | 879MB/s | 
| ATTO | Read | 1.89GB/s | 994MB/s | 
| Row 10 - Cell 0 | Write | 1.73GB/s | 906MB/s | 
| PCMark Data Drive Bench | Score | 2028 | 1250 | 
Let’s be brutally honest: USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 was a dead standard walking from its inception, and USB4 didn’t really include it in its repertoire of supported prior standards. There are a few exceptions, but in general, if you don’t actually have a port to the 2x2 standard, then you won’t see the true performance that this drive can muster.
For that reason, I’ve presented the performance via a Gen 2x2 port and a much more common Gen 2 variety. How does it compare with the best Gen 2x2 drives?
Well, read speed is below the Crucial X10 Pro, ADATA Elite SE880 and LaCie Rugged Mini SSD, but write speed is close to what all those achieve.
Given the different controllers and implementations of Gen 2x2 interfaces, the Fanxiang PS2000W portable SSD doesn’t have a compelling reason to be chosen over any other drive in Gen 2x2 mode, but it can get close to the maximum realistic speed for this interface.
But if speed is the prerequisite, then a USB4 or Thunderbolt external drive, like the Corsair EX400U or the SanDisk Extreme PRO with USB4, would be a better choice if you have a USB4 port. These drives can hit read speeds of 3800MB/s or higher, and 3650MB/s writes.
And, if I were rushing to catch a plane or train, and needed to transfer files, I know which I’d prefer.
- Performance: 4 / 5
Fanxiang PS2000W: Final verdict
If the Fanxiang PS2000W portable SSD had appeared during the golden age of Gen 2x2, when the Kingston XS2000 appeared back in early 2022, and at a reasonable price, then it might have been something I’d recommend.
And the fine irony of that comparison is that the price of the PS2000W is almost exactly the same as the XS2000's MSRP was nearly four years ago. And the Kingston device supported hardware encryption, where the Fanxiang does not.
To be clear, the construction quality and performance of the PS2000W are absolutely fine, but what isn’t is the amount of money being asked for.
If money isn’t an issue for you, I’d buy the Crucial X10 Pro before they’re extinct, as it has hardware encryption. Or I’d consider a USB4-capable drive, like the Corsair EX400U, if you have a port that supports that specification.
Should I buy the Fanxiang PS2000W?
| Value | 100% more expensive than it was 8 months ago | 3 / 5 | 
| Design | Metal construction, comes with a carry pouch and a dual standard cable | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | Works well at Gen 2x2 speeds, if you have that port | 4 / 5 | 
| Overall | A nice drive, but hardly great value | 3.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You have USB 3.2 Gen 2x2
If you have a USB port that is Gen 2x2 (not just Gen 2), then this might be the drive you want to exploit the extra speed that it offers. However, unless all the ports you are likely to plug it into are this spec, the advantage will be limited.  
Money isn’t a concern
Buying RAM, storage or GPUs is currently only for those people not paying with their own money. Since, depending on what you are buying, the price hikes range from 100% up to 400% and higher, if you can wait for the AI bubble to burst, you could save yourself, or your business, lots of money.
Don't buy it if...
You have USB 4.0
If you have USB4 or Thunderbolt 4, then this isn’t the drive for you, at whatever price. There are USB4-specified drives that are twice the speed of this one, and most of them only cost a little more.
You need bigger than 4TB
The largest drive available in this range is 4TB. And those wanting 8TB or more need to look for a different product entirely.
Also consider
Nextorage NX-PS1PRO Series
One of the first USB 4.0 capable external SSDs available, the Nextorage NX-PS1PRO Series comes in 1TB, 2TB or 4TB capacities.
Read our full Nextorage NX-PS1PRO Series review
OWC Envoy Pro FX
If you have Thunderbolt 3 ports or intend to add this functionality soon, then the Envoy Pro FX might well be worth your time. A beautifully engineered external storage option that can provide exceptional performance in the right circumstances, the OWC Envoy Pro FX is effective if expensive.
Read our full OWC Envoy Pro FX review
We've also tested out the fastest external SSDs around.
Mark is an expert on 3D printers, drones and phones. He also covers storage, including SSDs, NAS drives and portable hard drives. He started writing in 1986 and has contributed to MicroMart, PC Format, 3D World, among others.
